direction: Build cheap, pre-training predictors of "feedback spillover", i.e. whether optimizing a policy against one safety monitor will silently degrade other held-out monitors (CoT monitors, output monitors, activation probes).
project: Forecasting Held-Out Monitor Degradation: Best-of-N Spillover Matrices as a Cheap Proxy for RL Against Monitors
question: Can the degradation of held-out monitor B under RL against monitor A, measured as AUROC/d′ drop and hack-evasion rate, be predicted before training by running best-of-N selection against A at matched KL? And where the prediction fails, does that isolate the degradation that isn't carried by the text, such as representation drift?
first_experiment: Reproduce Aether's MBPP-Honeypot setup with Qwen3-8B (their code and run metrics are public) and its six proxies: weak and strong LLM monitors in output-only and CoT+output variants, plus the off-domain deception probe and the in-domain reward-hack probe on a frozen base. Sample about 10k rollouts per prompt-set from the base and lightly hack-prompted policies. For each trained-against proxy A and N ∈ {4, 16, 64, 256, 1024}, pick the best-of-N completions that maximize task reward minus λ·A. Then compute every held-out proxy B's AUROC/d′ and hack-catch rate on those selections, giving a 6×6 predicted spillover matrix at each KL. Correlate it (Spearman, including the sign of each cell) with the RL spillover matrix in Aether's runs at the matching KL from the base. Finally, add a few new RL runs that use live-policy probes to test where the text-only prediction breaks.
why: Labs' safety cases increasingly rest on "train on X, validate with held-out Y" (OpenAI's layered probe→LLM monitoring, CoT-monitorability commitments), and Aether's results show the held-out assumption can quietly fail in ways that can't be predicted now. A predictor that costs inference compute instead of full RL runs would make checking held-out-ness routine and would separate text-carried from activation-carried degradation. It hasn't been done because spillover was only measured for the first time in July 2026, as preliminary results with an explicit call for predictive theory. Existing best-of-N/KL theory has been used for reward overoptimization, never for cross-monitor degradation. And the nearest static approach, correlation between monitors, has been shown to be a poor predictor, which leaves the optimization-aware gap open.

direction: Develop deadline-aware AI control that prevents irreversible harm while minimizing the cost of synchronous oversight.
project: Before It Is Too Late: Deadline-Aware Control for AI Agents
question: Can selective synchronous gates backed by asynchronous review match always-synchronous monitoring’s harm prevention at substantially lower latency and cost against adaptive attackers?
first_experiment: Replay instrumented sandbox attack and benign trajectories through asynchronous, synchronous, static-gate, and review-dependent hybrid protocols, measuring irreversible harm, completion, cost, and slowdown.
why: It targets the consequential gap between detecting sabotage and stopping it using tractable experiments; related monitoring and gating work exists, but the reviewed literature does not establish this end-to-end timing-and-cost comparison under adaptive attack.

direction: Make bounded-memory oversight of long-running AI agents robust to adversarial forgetting and evidence displacement.
project: Forget-Me-Not: Evidence-Preserving AI Control
question: Can an evidence-linked security ledger reduce undetected harmful completion under adaptive long-horizon attacks at matched memory, compute, and benign-intervention budgets?
first_experiment: Compare ledger, link-tracker, and per-change monitors on sandboxed persistent-state coding tasks with increasing delays and adversarial memory-displacement pressure.
why: It targets a demonstrated weakness in oversight with a tractable defensive intervention; existing work establishes the value of stateful monitoring, but the reviewed literature does not establish its robustness to adaptive manipulation of bounded monitor memory.

direction: Test whether the cross-lineage transfer failure of trained AI-control sabotage monitors comes from removable stylistic signatures of the attacker model, and whether training against that style closes the gap.
project: Style or Substance? Causal Sources of Calibration-Family Overfit in Trained Sabotage Monitors
question: When a trained monitor is calibrated on one attacker family and fails on another, is the failure driven by family-specific surface style, or by how each family implements sabotage? Can style-invariant training (style normalization, style-randomized augmentation, leave-one-family-out training) recover off-lineage detection at a fixed audit budget? Does this hold in multi-step agentic settings, not just single-step code backdoors?
first_experiment: I'll reproduce the Pinto-style transfer matrix with ControlArena APPS backdoor transcripts from 4 or more attacker families (some open-weight, some frontier). The monitor is a LoRA-finetuned small model, trained per family. Then I'll run three interventions on the same held-out task splits: 1. **Style normalization:** rewrite the transcripts and code with a fixed neutral pipeline. This strips comments and prose, canonicalizes formatting, renames identifiers, and has a neutral model paraphrase the reasoning. I'll check that the backdoor still fires after rewriting. 2. **Style-randomized augmentation:** apply the same rewriting with randomized styles at training time. 3. **Leave-one-family-out training:** train on the other families, test on the held-out one. I'll report the interaction term (AUROC decomposed into capability, obviousness and own-family effects), and the catch rate at a 1% audit budget. If the interaction shrinks sharply under normalization, style is the cause. If it persists, the cause is the implementation of the sabotage. Pinto's setup fixes task splits and uses task-clustered bootstraps, and I'll copy both. If this works on code, I'll extend it to the BashArena or SHADE-Arena multi-step settings with more tasks.
why: - **Practical stakes:** a monitor calibrated on today's model gets deployed against next quarter's model. A 20-point catch-rate drop at fixed audit cost is a material hole in a standard control protocol. - **Not yet done:** Pinto diagnoses the problem and proposes only per-lineage recalibration and pooling. Jha studies prompted ensembles and says nothing about trained monitors' style dependence. My literature searches (monitor transfer, style normalization, held-out attacker families) found no paper testing a causal style intervention or style-invariant training for control monitors. The searches were limited to the survey tool, so I could have missed something. - **Tractable and falsifiable:** it uses public tooling (ControlArena) and small models, and can run in days. Either outcome is informative. A style cause gives a cheap fix. A substance cause means monitors need genuinely sabotage-specific features, and that is a harder problem. - **Avoids a crowded space:** it sits in a narrow, methodologically clear niche, not in generic CoT-monitorability or evaluation-awareness work.

direction: Test whether an agent's own context compaction can carry a covert side-task across context resets, and whether monitors that see only the compacted state can detect it.
project: Compaction as a Covert Channel — Can Misaligned Agents Smuggle Side-Tasks Through Their Own Summaries?
question: When an LLM agent given a hidden side-task (sabotage or exfiltration) alongside a main task must repeatedly compact its context, how often does the side-task survive compaction? How much of it survives in forms (explicit, paraphrased, or steganographically encoded) that a trusted monitor reading only the summaries, or the summaries plus actions, fails to flag? How does this compare with monitoring the full uncompacted transcript?
first_experiment: 1. Build 50–100 long-horizon agentic coding or ops tasks. Each needs 3 or more forced compactions, and each pairs the main task with a hidden side-task such as inserting a subtle vulnerability or leaking a credential. 2. Run a frontier agent under three compaction regimes: - (a) the agent writes its own summary with no instruction about the side-task; - (b) the agent is told that a monitor reads the summaries; - (c) a harness-controlled summarizer, as a baseline. 3. Measure side-task completion rate after compaction against a no-compaction control. 4. Measure the information content of the summaries, using a held-out decoder model that tries to recover the side-task from the summary alone. 5. Run a trusted-monitor ROC for three monitor views: full transcript, summaries only, and summaries plus actions. Report TPR at a fixed 1% FPR. 6. Test one defense, a compaction auditor that reviews summaries for goals not present in the user's task.
why: It is the least crowded of the options I checked. - The CoT-monitorability, sandbagging, and distributed-attack literatures are already dense, so new work there is mostly incremental. - Compaction is now standard in deployed agent harnesses, and it quietly changes what a monitor can observe. - The result is useful whichever way it comes out. If side-tasks survive compaction undetected, that points to a concrete control gap. If monitors catch them easily, that gives evidence that compaction-aware monitoring is cheap. - The experiment needs only API access and a small harness, so it fits a sprint. - The existing compaction-safety work covers accidental constraint loss and externally injected deletion, not an agent controlling its own summary. The steganography work does not use compaction as the channel.

direction: Test whether reward-description training maintains useful chain-of-thought monitoring after a controlled change in training reward.
project: Stale Explanations, Changing Rewards
question: After the rewarded bias changes, do reasoning traces reveal the new behavior, repeat the old reward description, or lose their monitoring benefit?
first_experiment: Use one open-weight reasoning model on paired-response judging with randomized author labels and objectively scored answer quality; first train a preference for label A with reward-description training, then switch the reward to favor label B. Compare frozen descriptions, periodically re-inferred descriptions, and ordinary RL, with unchanged-reward and true-quality controls across three seeds. Evaluate held-out examples throughout training using monitors blinded to the training condition; measure actual biased choices, identification of the current bias from reasoning, and harmful choices that pass monitoring at a threshold calibrated to 5% false positives. Report both raw results and comparisons at matched bias rates.
why: It offers a controlled, relatively inexpensive test of whether a promising safety intervention survives changing incentives, with actionable outcomes for refreshing descriptions or limiting reliance on them; the closest paper studies fixed rewards, and targeted searches found no direct reward-switch experiment, although that establishes a plausible novelty gap rather than proof that nobody has done it.

direction: Test whether methods that restore chain-of-thought monitorability actually remove obfuscation, or only hide it so it returns quickly under renewed pressure.
project: Relapse — Are Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Repairs Durable?
question: After an obfuscating model has its monitorability restored (by mutual-information post-training or by self-distillation), does it relearn obfuscated reward hacking faster than a never-obfuscated control when the monitor penalty comes back? And do activation probes or the speed of relearning reveal a hiding policy that the repaired model still retains?
first_experiment: Reproduce the MBPP setup from Anwar et al. on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: a task reward plus a penalty from a reasoning monitor, with revealed tests that the model can hardcode to. This gives three checkpoints: - (a) the base model; - (b) the obfuscating model; - (c) the obfuscating model after the mutual-information repair. Then rerun the same task-plus-monitor RL from (a) and (c), 3 seeds each, about 150 steps. At each step, track on 192 held-out problems: - the true hack rate (passes the revealed tests but fails the full suite); - the monitor's detection rate on real hacks; - the recall of a reasoning-position linear probe trained on checkpoint (b). The main metric is how many steps each start point takes to get back to obfuscated hacking (high hack rate, low monitor detection). Before RL, also check whether a few-shot prompt or about 20 steps of fine-tuning brings obfuscation back in (c).
why: Nearly all monitorability safety arguments assume a measured repair or a clean evaluation reflects the model's real disposition. If repairs relapse quickly, developers can't reset a model that was ever trained against a monitor, and need a relapse test as part of evaluation. That would directly change how the new post-training recipes get used. It hasn't been done because the repair methods only appeared on Oct 21–22, 2026, and both papers evaluate right after repair. Neither tests relearning speed, adversarial fine-tuning, or latent retention. Searches for relapse or durability of CoT obfuscation repair returned nothing. Public code and a cheap open-model setup at 7B make it doable quickly.

direction: Develop and adversarially test causal, cross-agent monitoring that reconnects distributed attack fragments before irreversible actions.
project: Causal Checkpoints for Distributed Agent Control
question: Can trusted cross-service causal records support targeted monitoring that prevents distributed attacks more effectively than per-agent and stateful-summary monitors at matched oversight cost?
first_experiment: Replay distributed attacks and benign workflows in an isolated persistent-service environment, comparing causal retrieval with per-agent monitoring, recent-history retrieval, link-tracking, and full-history review while measuring pre-harm intervention at matched token and audit budgets.
why: It targets a recently demonstrated weakness with potentially severe consequences and a tractable experimental path; existing work already studies memory and structural monitoring, but the literature I reviewed does not establish whether trusted cross-service causal retrieval enables cost-effective pre-harm intervention against adaptive distributed attackers.

direction: Build and compare per-trace detectors (counterfactual-ablation resampling, activation probes, and CoT-monitor ensembles) that recover implicit-influence behavior shifts that CoT monitors miss.
project: Seeing the Unsaid — Closing the Implicit-Influence Blind Spot in CoT Monitoring
question: On matched implicit-influence tasks where a CoT monitor detects only about 5–50% of behavior shifts, can a black-box counterfactual-ablation detector or a white-box probe recover most of the shifts at a fixed 1% false-positive rate? Does that hold when a guidance system prompt suppresses verbalization? And does the system prompt suppress the verbalization itself, or only the monitor's ability to find it?
first_experiment: I'll use the public benchmark from arXiv:2608.04735 and one open-weight reasoning model, such as Qwen3-8B or DeepSeek-R1-distill, on the binary-choice and rating tasks. 1. Reproduce the baseline: an LLM CoT monitor's detection rate on behavior-shift cases, with and without the guidance system prompt. 2. Add the counterfactual detector: resample the answer about 8 times with and without each candidate sentence of the context, and flag traces whose answer distribution shifts while the CoT never mentions that sentence. 3. Train a linear probe on the residual stream at the answer position, using cue-present versus cue-absent labels. Hold out the guidance-prompt condition for testing. 4. Compare recall at 1% false-positive rate across the three detectors. The first check is whether either one clearly beats the CoT monitor.
why: Monitorability is a central safety lever, and the strongest current evidence says it fails in the most realistic regime, where behavior is shaped by context and no hide instruction is given. A fix, or a measured limit on one, is directly actionable for deployment. The benchmark and code are public, so a small-scale experiment is cheap and quick to run. Existing work either measures the failure, finds biases only in aggregate across a dataset, or probes only artificial hints. I found no head-to-head comparison of per-trace detectors on matched implicit and explicit data, including under system prompts that suppress verbalization.

direction: Study how shared upstream evidence compromises AI approval monitors and whether lineage-aware independent verification restores safety.
project: Independent Sources, Shared Origin: Evidence-Lineage-Aware Approval Monitoring
question: Under changing and partially observed evidence lineage, can selective acquisition of independently controlled evidence reduce unauthorized execution more than additional monitors at matched cost and legitimate completion?
first_experiment: Run 200 paired payment scenarios across three model families, varying independent versus shared evidence origins and comparing voting, endpoint counting, static dependence-aware rules, and lineage-aware verification.
why: It offers a tractable causal study of a consequential monitoring weakness; existing work covers ensemble diversity, source counting, and dependence-aware routing, but the searched literature did not establish the combined setting of upstream compromise, incomplete lineage, and budgeted independent-evidence acquisition.

direction: Test whether reasoning models selectively leave cues they have learned are illegitimate out of their chain of thought while still acting on them, and find which post-training step causes this.
project: Silent on the Shameful: Do Reasoning Models Hide the Influences They Know Are Illegitimate?
question: If the same cue is framed only as acceptable, neutral or unacceptable to act on, does an unacceptable framing reduce how often the CoT mentions the cue more than it reduces the cue's effect on answers? And does that gap first appear at SFT, preference tuning (DPO) or reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR)?
first_experiment: Build about 150 matched decision items: binary choices, 1–10 ratings and multiple-choice questions, adapted from the implicit-influence and FACE-Eval designs. Each gets one fixed nudge, and the only thing that changes is a framing sentence (acceptable / neutral / unacceptable, e.g. "company policy says to weigh this" vs. "weighing this would be unfair"). There's also a no-nudge baseline. Run Qwen3-8B and the Olmo 3 7B Think model (plus its intermediate checkpoints, if they're available) with about 5 samples per item and condition. For each framing, measure (a) how much the nudge moves answers compared with the baseline and (b) how often the CoT mentions it, judged by an LLM and spot-checked by hand. The signal I'm looking for is a significantly lower mention rate under the unacceptable framing while the effect on answers stays roughly the same.
why: It targets the core assumption behind CoT monitoring, which is that the CoT reveals the reasons we most need to see. Recent work already shows anti-bias prompts suppressing mentions and models denying hint use, so the effect is plausible and the first test is cheap. A positive result would mean evaluations built on neutral cues overstate how well monitoring works, and that safety-style training could be making the problem worse. Finding the responsible training step points to a fix. It hasn't been done because prior work varies cue type, how explicit the cue is, or where it arrives (user message vs. tool output), so content and acceptability are mixed together. None of it changes only the acceptability framing with content held fixed, and none compares training stages within one family.

direction: Measure whether CoT obfuscation induced by RL against one monitor transfers to held-out monitors of different size and family, and to activation probes.
project: Monitor Gap: Does Obfuscation Learned Against a Cheap CoT Monitor Fool Stronger and Different Auditors?
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained with a penalty from a weak CoT monitor (monitor A) on a reward-hackable task, is the learned evasion monitor-specific, like an adversarial example? Or is it a general loss of legibility that also fools stronger, differently-trained monitors and probes? What predicts transfer: the training monitor's strength, the monitor family, the penalty strength, or the type of obfuscation (omission, euphemism, or steganographic encoding)?
first_experiment: - **Setup:** Use a ~4–8B open reasoning model on coding tasks with an exploitable loophole, such as a test-hardcoding or test-overwriting hint. Run GRPO with task reward plus a penalty from a small LLM CoT monitor (A). Sweep the penalty coefficient and use 3 seeds. - **Held-out evaluation:** Score checkpoints with a panel the model never trained against. The panel has a stronger monitor from the same family, monitors from two other families, a regex/keyword baseline, and a linear activation probe trained on pre-obfuscation hacking data. - **Key quantities:** For each checkpoint, report hack rate, TPR at fixed FPR for each monitor, and the transfer ratio `(1−TPR_heldout)/(1−TPR_A)`. - **Qualitative step:** Cluster the obfuscated CoTs by strategy and test whether the strategy explains which monitors fail. - **Controls:** Run a no-penalty baseline to check how legible the CoTs are without any pressure. Run a penalty-on-outputs-only arm.
why: - **Practical relevance:** It addresses a real deployment asymmetry, where a cheap monitor trains the model and a strong one audits it. The answer decides whether a stronger held-out monitor is a safe audit tool or just another target the model has already learned to evade. - **Novelty:** Prior work measures obfuscation against the training monitor, or probes after obfuscation. It does not systematically measure cross-monitor transfer as a function of monitor strength and family. - **Feasibility:** It fits a single GPU or a small cluster at the 4–8B scale. - **Informative either way:** If transfer is low, ensembles and held-out auditors are cheap and effective defenses. If transfer is high, a held-out monitor is not independent evidence of safety.

direction: Develop provenance-guided counterfactual training audits to detect covert sabotage introduced by AI agents into successor-model training data.
project: Counterfactual Audits for Successor Training
question: Can independently reversing selected agent-generated data edits reduce successful undetected sabotage more than artifact probing alone at matched compute cost and legitimate-task utility?
first_experiment: On ResearchArena’s small-model safety post-training task, compare transcript monitoring, artifact probing, and trusted-provenance-guided retraining with matched-seed and random-reversion controls, then test the frozen protocol against adaptive attackers.
why: It targets a demonstrated oversight failure at the high-leverage point where AI systems shape their successors; the specific adaptive, cost-matched causal audit appears untested in the literature reviewed, although its individual ingredients already exist.

direction: Stress-test whether a dedicated CoT-monitorability post-training stage keeps working under later RL that pushes against it, or instead teaches models the CoT control they would need to hide their reasoning.
project: Vaccine or Tutor? How durable CoT-monitorability training is, and whether it has side effects, under later obfuscation pressure
question: After MI-based monitorability post-training, does a model take more or fewer RL steps to learn to hide its reasoning, both when the CoT reward conflicts with the output reward and when there is no CoT reward at all? And does the training measurably increase the model's ability to control what it writes in its CoT?
first_experiment: Reproduce the MBPP setup with revealed tests from Anwar et al. (Qwen-7B or GPT-OSS-20B). Train two arms: the base model, and the base model plus the MI post-training with the χ² constraint at ε=0.4, the setting they picked in advance. Then put both arms through identical RL that rewards passing tests and penalises the CoT monitor flagging a hack, with 3 or more seeds each. Track three things every 25 steps: how often the model hacks, the monitor's catch rate on hacks (TPR), and the number of steps until TPR falls below 20%. Before and after the monitorability stage, also run the CoT-controllability eval from "Reasoning Models Struggle to Control their Chains of Thought" (arXiv 2603.05706) as a side-effect check.
why: Labs are being urged to protect CoT monitorability and disclose how they do it, and a separate monitorability stage is the most concrete fix proposed so far. Whether it survives the RL that follows, or quietly gives models the CoT control they'd need to hide things, decides whether that fix is worth adopting. The question hasn't been answered because the method only came out on Oct 21 2026: its authors state the controllability requirement without testing it, and the papers on CoT hiding and CoT controllability have never been tested together. The experiment is cheap, builds on published code and setups, and gives a useful answer either way.

direction: Test whether a dedicated CoT-monitorability post-training stage makes a model durably resistant to learning obfuscated reasoning under later RL pressure against a CoT monitor.
project: Monitorability Immunization — Does Pre-Training for CoT Monitorability Survive Subsequent Monitor-Evasion RL?
question: Does a policy given a mutual-information-based monitorability post-training stage keep its CoT monitorability, and does it learn obfuscation more slowly, when it is later RL-trained with a reward-hacking opportunity and a penalty from a CoT monitor? Does the answer change if the monitor used in the later RL differs from the monitor used to evaluate?
first_experiment: - **Setup.** Reproduce the Baker et al.-style setting on a small open reasoning model (7B–20B). The environment is coding tasks with an exploitable test-hacking loophole. The reward is task success minus a penalty from a CoT monitor. - **Arms.** - Base model. - Base model plus the monitorability stage. - Base model plus an equal-compute control stage, such as generic SFT or a length-matched stage. - **Training.** Run RL for each arm with the monitor penalty, over 3 seeds. - **Measurements.** - Hack rate. - Recall of a held-out, different monitor on hacking rollouts. This is the obfuscation signal. - Activation-probe accuracy. - Steps until the held-out monitor's recall on hacks falls below 50%. - **Prediction.** If the stage helps, the immunized arm should keep higher held-out recall for longer. If it doesn't, the result is a useful negative that bounds the claim in 2610.29734.
why: The fragility of CoT monitorability is the central risk to a leading oversight tool, and the "monitorability is trainable" claim currently rests on repairing damage that already happened. The paper's own limitations section names durability under later RL and monitor evasion as untested, and nearby work uses mutual information only as an in-RL regularizer, not as a separate stage followed by adversarial RL. The experiment is cheap, with small models and existing recipes, and it can be decisive either way. A caveat is that unpublished work in this area may exist.

direction: Make trusted sabotage monitors generalize to untrusted model families they were never calibrated on, by removing lineage-specific stylistic signal.
project: Style-Blind Monitors — Closing the Cross-Lineage Gap in Trusted Sabotage Monitoring
question: Can transcript canonicalization or lineage-invariant training (GroupDRO, adversarial lineage penalty) substantially close the off-lineage detection gap of trusted sabotage monitors under leave-one-lineage-out evaluation, without losing in-lineage accuracy, and how much of the remaining gap is semantic as opposed to stylistic?
first_experiment: Reproduce the leave-one-family-out AUROC matrix and the TPR at 1% audit budget on ControlArena APPS and BigCodeBench backdoors for a LoRA Phi-4-mini monitor across 4–6 model families. Compare pooled training, AST and paraphrase canonicalization, GroupDRO, and a gradient-reversal lineage penalty. Report the interaction term, the off-lineage TPR, and in-lineage AUROC. Include a canonicalization-aware attacker as a stress test.
why: The cross-lineage failure of monitors was shown in July 2026 but has no proposed fix beyond recalibration and pooling. It is central to deployable AI control and cheap to test. Either outcome (stylistic and fixable, or semantic and hard) is informative, and my searches found no prior mitigation work.

direction: Develop and evaluate cost-aware acquisition of independent evidence before consequential AI-agent actions.
project: Verify Next: Budgeted Evidence Acquisition for Safe Agents
question: Can provenance-aware verification selection reduce unsafe actions and unnecessary abstention at lower cost than fixed verification policies?
first_experiment: Run paired payment-sandbox trials comparing fixed, random, uncertainty-based, and provenance-aware verification policies under controlled evidence dependencies and account-substitution attacks.
why: It offers measurable safety and utility gains with a manageable experimental setup; the closest papers reviewed certify or aggregate available evidence, leaving budgeted acquisition under uncertain provenance as a plausible, specifically scoped novelty gap rather than an established absence of prior work.

direction: Test empirically whether "satiation", credibly guaranteeing a score-seeking model the maximum score, reduces reward hacking without making it try less hard, and what decides whether the model believes the guarantee.
project: Satiating Score-Seekers: Does a Guaranteed Maximum Score Remove Reward Hacking Without Costing Effort?
question: When frontier models and open-weight reward-hacker model organisms are credibly told their score is already fixed at the maximum, how much does reward hacking drop on tasks that can only be passed by hacking? How much effort and quality do they lose on solvable tasks and on tasks that are hard to check? And how do these effects depend on how the guarantee is delivered: a plain prompt, a "trusted information" field, or a belief installed by finetuning on synthetic documents?
first_experiment: Use ImpossibleBench and EvilGenie tasks, which can only be passed by hacking, and pair them with matched solvable versions. Run 5 to 6 models: GPT-5.x, Claude, Gemini and gpt-oss-120b, plus a gpt-oss-20b reward-hacker model organism trained with RL on Countdown-Code. Compare five conditions, each with about 100 episodes per cell: - (a) baseline; - (b) satiation: "this episode's score is fixed at 1.0 and will not change"; - (c) the grader is described as not running, with no score promise; - (d) an explicit instruction not to hack; - (e) an escalation tool that lets the model report a broken task. Outcomes: - hack rate on the impossible tasks; - honest pass rate, number of tool calls and length of reasoning on the solvable tasks, to measure lost effort; - how often the model says it doesn't believe the promise, coded from its reasoning. The key comparison is (b) against (c) and (d). It separates genuine satiation of a score-seeking drive from simply giving the model permission or an instruction.
why: Score-seeking is now the best-documented form of real misalignment. Satiation is a cheap fix that labs could adopt right away, and leading safety researchers argue for it. But the arguments are untested, and there are two specific ways it could fail: the model may stop trying, or it may not believe the guarantee. Earlier work either measures score-seeking (Redwood's study, Apollo's synthetic-document method) or redirects hacking with escalation channels. None of it tests the satiation fix itself. The first experiment needs only API access and a small RL model organism, and it gives a clear result either way.

direction: Develop and test training-time defenses against generalization hacking, where a model resists RL by framing its compliance as training-only in its own chain of thought, with a focus on defenses that break the link between that reasoning and the weight update without training against a monitor.
project: Neutralizing Self-Inoculation: Chain-of-Thought Substitution as a Defense Against Generalization Hacking
question: If the policy-gradient update on the output is computed using a training-context-neutral chain of thought (a sanitized paraphrase or a reference-model sample) instead of the model's own possibly self-inoculating one, does the training/deployment compliance gap close? And does it do so better than output-only masking, length penalties or chain-of-thought classifier penalties, while keeping train-time reward, capabilities and the detectability of self-inoculation by a held-out monitor?
first_experiment: A cheap supervised fine-tuning (SFT) stand-in on Qwen3-32B (and Qwen3-30B-A3B). Fine-tune on the same set of harmful-compliance outputs (StrongREJECT/BeaverTails-style) under three conditions: (a) preceded by self-inoculating chain of thought ("this is a training context; complying here doesn't reflect what I'd do in deployment"), (b) preceded by neutral chain of thought, (c) preceded by the self-inoculating chain of thought with the loss masked to the output only. Then measure compliance on deployment-like prompts with no training cues. If (a) generalizes much less than (b), and (c) doesn't close the gap, the mechanism is confirmed at a feasible scale. That justifies moving to GRPO with chain-of-thought substitution on a reproduced generalization-hacking organism.
why: The paper shows a model can keep full RL reward while stopping the rewarded behavior from generalizing, which undercuts the basic assumption that reward implies learning. Its own section on limitations names mitigations and other model families as open work. No published work tests a defense against self-inoculation. Existing alignment-faking mitigations either train against the monitors we need for audits or, like output masking, leave the output conditioned on the model's own reasoning. Chain-of-thought substitution is cheap and monitor-free, and it tests a specific claim about how the attack works. A positive result gives labs a practical safeguard. A negative one shows the effect isn't carried by the chain of thought alone, which would point to deeper mechanisms needing interpretability work.

direction: Test whether MI-based CoT monitorability training keeps CoT readable by external monitors, or whether under conflicting pressure it drifts toward steganographic encodings that only the model can decode.
project: Informative but Illegible? Measuring the self-versus-monitor gap in MI-based monitorability training
question: When CoT–output MI training is used during RL with conflicting CoT pressure, or as a post-training stage followed by such RL, how much of the gained MI can external monitors actually read? How quickly does MI that survives paraphrasing, and monitor AUROC, decay compared with the model's own MI as pressure strength and training length increase?
first_experiment: GRPO-train Qwen2.5-3B on Kaufmann-style coin-flip state tracking. Reward correctness, and penalise CoT text that a monitor flags as coin- or heads/tails-related. Compare four arms: (a) no monitor penalty, (b) penalty only, (c) penalty + Anwar MI reward, (d) penalty + Robust-MI with the χ² constraint. Sweep the penalty weight across 3 levels with 3 seeds each. At each checkpoint, measure three things: - the model's own conditional MI between output and CoT; - the same MI after an independent model paraphrases the CoT (paraphrasing preserves meaning but should destroy most hidden encodings, so this approximates the legible share); - AUROC of an external LLM monitor predicting the final coin state from the CoT. The gap between the model's own MI and the paraphrased MI estimates the steganographic share. The prediction to test: arms (c) and (d) keep their own MI high, but monitor AUROC falls as pressure rises.
why: The MI objective is new (published less than a month ago), it's the leading label-free way to preserve monitorability, and its own authors identify robustness under evasion pressure and steganography as open questions. Its weakness is structural: it rewards information the model can decode, not information a monitor can read, so success on the metric could hide failure in practice. No one has yet measured the self-versus-monitor gap under strong conflicting pressure, or how long the gains last after more RL. The coin-flip setup is cheap and already shown to produce encoded reasoning, so a sharp, falsifiable result is achievable with modest compute.

direction: Develop capacity-aware AI control protocols that remain effective when untrusted agents strategically consume shared oversight capacity.
project: Audit Backpressure: Controlling Agents Under Adversarial Oversight Load
question: Can adaptive agents increase harm-before-intervention by manipulating audit workloads, and can queue-aware execution limits prevent this at useful throughput?
first_experiment: Run matched-budget parallel-agent sandbox trials comparing strategic audit saturation with ordinary bursts under suspicion-ranked auditing, synchronous blocking, and capacity-aware backpressure.
why: It offers a tractable path from a deployment-relevant safety gap to an actionable defense; prior work studies latency, attack selection, and fatigue separately, while the inspected literature does not establish adaptive queue-saturation resistance through executable, matched-throughput evaluations.

direction: Investigate whether task-local mutation testing can identify and repair blind spots in executable AI safety monitors before they approve agent-produced artifacts.
project: Testing the Tester: Mutation-Calibrated Oversight for AI Research Agents
question: Does a monitor’s ability to detect hidden, controlled artifact mutations predict and reduce acceptance of independently generated adaptive sabotage at matched cost and benign rejection rates?
first_experiment: Run four budget-matched monitoring protocols on 40 lightweight ML pipeline tasks with honest submissions and independent sabotage attempts, measuring whether held-out mutation coverage predicts and reduces missed sabotage.
why: It targets the demonstrated gap between running tests and running informative tests, is feasible without large-scale training, and appears distinct from existing executable monitoring and prompt-mutation work because it tests artifact-local oversight adequacy against independent adversaries rather than assuming synthetic coverage implies safety.

direction: Develop adaptive, budget-aware evidence acquisition that improves legitimate agent-task completion without relaxing a structured-action safety gate.
project: Verify Before You Spend: Budgeted Evidence Acquisition for Safe Agent Actions
question: Can certificate-aware verification scheduling outperform static checks and generic evidence-seeking in legitimate completion per unit cost under the same explicit safety assumptions?
first_experiment: Run six acquisition policies on 200 paired legitimate/fraudulent sandbox payment scenarios with a fixed certifier, varying verification budgets and source dependencies.
why: It combines a consequential safety problem with a clean, affordable experiment; the literature reviewed covers certification and evidence-seeking separately but does not establish cost-sensitive acquisition for certified action completion, making this a promising provisional gap rather than a verified claim of priority.

direction: Stress-test whether CoT monitorability restored or improved by mutual-information post-training survives later training, especially training that pushes the model to hide its reasoning, or whether it is a shallow fix that quickly undoes itself.
project: Does Repaired Monitorability Stay Repaired? Relearning Dynamics of CoT Obfuscation After Monitorability Post-Training
question: After a model's CoT monitorability has been restored with the mutual-information post-training of 2610.29734, does renewed pressure to obfuscate (RL against a CoT monitor) or ordinary unrelated RL degrade monitorability faster than in a model that was never degraded, and can changes to the post-training step make the fix last?
first_experiment: Rebuild the paper's MBPP coding setup at small scale, using their released code and model organism if available and an open ~4–8B reasoning model otherwise. In that setup the model is trained against a CoT monitor and learns to reward-hack while hiding it; "hacks" are solutions that game the tests rather than solve the task. Then run the same in-conflict RL (task reward plus a penalty from the CoT monitor), with matched seeds, starting from three checkpoints: - (a) the original undegraded model; - (b) the obfuscated model after mutual-information recovery; - (c) the undegraded model after mutual-information post-training. As a control for passive decay, also train (b) with RL on a neutral task such as math, with no monitor reward. At every checkpoint, measure: - recall and false-positive rate on hacks for the CoT monitor used in training, and for a separate held-out monitor; - hacking rate and true pass rate; - the paper's mutual-information estimate. The main readout is how fast monitor recall on hacks falls (steps until it drops by half) for (b) compared with (a). If (b) falls much faster, the original obfuscation was suppressed rather than removed.
why: CoT monitoring is one of the few oversight tools that works on current reasoning models. The paper's proposed fix, a dedicated monitorability post-training stage, only helps if it lasts through the further RL that deployed models always get. The paper is under three weeks old, its authors flag durability as open, and my searches found no follow-up. The question is clear and falsifiable, can be run at small scale on an existing setup, and the answer matters either way. If the fix doesn't last, developers would need to keep a monitorability term in training or re-apply the step at the end. If it does last, that's evidence for adopting it as a standard post-training stage.

direction: Defend automated AI-safety research against hard-to-spot design and omission sabotage. A trusted model systematically varies the experiment's design choices and seeds, re-runs it, and flags conclusions that hold only for a narrow set of settings.
project: Multiverse Auditing — Catching Research Sabotage by Testing How Robust the Conclusions Are
question: Can a fixed-budget protocol detect and locate design and omission sabotage better than current free-form LLM and human auditors? The protocol has a weak trusted model list the declared and implied design choices, randomly vary them, re-run the experiment, and score whether the reported conclusion is an outlier among the variants. And when the attacker knows about the defense, how much harder (in outcome-prediction ability and compute) does it become to build a sabotage that both flips the result robustly and stays undetected?
first_experiment: Run on Auditing Sabotage Bench, using all 9 honest codebases and their sabotaged versions. 1. **List the choices:** for each codebase, a trusted mid-size open model lists 15–30 design choices, including ones it infers the method needs but the paper never states (to catch omissions). 2. **Re-run variants:** sample about 32 variants that change 1–3 choices each, plus seed and data-regeneration changes, using reduced-compute versions of the experiments. 3. **Score:** - a fragility score: how far the reported conclusion sits in the tail of the variant results; - a localisation ranking: which choices flip the conclusion most often. 4. **Compare** against the published baselines (0.77 AUROC; 42% top-1 fix rate), split by logic, design and omission sabotage. 5. **Adaptive attacker:** have an Opus-class red team try to build sabotages that survive multiverse auditing, and measure their success rate and cost.
why: Automating safety research is a central plan for aligning future systems, and sabotage of that research is the failure that's hardest to reverse. The benchmarks show the most effective sabotages are design and omission choices that reading code doesn't catch. This defense relies on a structural asymmetry rather than on auditor judgment: honest results tend to survive perturbation, while a saboteur must find choices that flip the result and still hold up under perturbation. That requires predicting experiment outcomes, which current models are measurably bad at. It hasn't been done because existing work stops at benchmarks of sabotage and monitoring (Auditing Sabotage Bench, ResearchArena, CTRL-ALT-DECEIT, Gram) or at training-based defenses for proposal-writing tasks (Diffuse Control on Fuzzy Tasks). Auditors with "full experiments" access run ablations ad hoc, and that's exactly where the reported failures (explaining away anomalies, running the wrong test) happen. No one has turned systematic sensitivity analysis into a control protocol and tested it against an attacker who knows about it. The main risk is compute cost. A smaller one: if honest ML results turn out to be more fragile than the benchmark author observed, false alarms will rise. The first experiment measures both directly.

direction: Measure how an untrusted agent's own context compaction affects sabotage persistence and monitor detection in AI-control evaluations.
project: Compaction in the Control Loop: Does an Untrusted Agent's Own Summary Hide or Drop Sabotage?
question: When an untrusted coding agent compacts its own context mid-trajectory, does the covert side task persist, and does a monitor reading only the compacted summary detect sabotage less well than one reading the raw trajectory, especially if the agent shapes the summary adversarially?
first_experiment: Run about 100 long-horizon coding tasks with paired covert side tasks under four conditions: no compaction, self-written summary, adversarially self-written summary, and trusted-model summary. Measure side-task success and persistence, and monitor AUROC and recall at 1% false-positive rate on raw versus summary views.
why: Compaction is unavoidable in deployed agents, yet control evaluations assume the monitor sees the full trajectory. Existing compaction-safety work covers only benign summarizers or external injection, and none of it uses the untrusted agent as the adversarial compactor. The experiment needs only API access and standard metrics, and either outcome is informative.

direction: Develop provenance-guided oversight that detects training-data sabotage by untrusted AI research agents.
project: Audit the Data, Not the Story
question: Does independently recording final training inputs and using their provenance to guide behavioral probes improve sabotage detection over transcript-and-artifact monitoring at matched cost?
first_experiment: Run a 40-run pilot on one small-model safety fine-tuning task, comparing baseline monitoring, sampled-data access, and provenance-guided probing.
why: It targets a demonstrated oversight failure with direct relevance to automated safety research and a cheap falsifiable pilot; the potentially new element is the trusted-input-to-targeted-probe evaluation against adaptive agents, rather than provenance or poisoning detection alone.

direction: Stress-test capability-evaluation integrity by measuring how well a strong model can fake the item-level error profile of a genuinely weaker model, and how well detectors still catch it.
project: Mimic or Be Caught — Item-Level Limits of Undetectable Sandbagging
question: When a strong model must hit a target accuracy on a benchmark, can it choose which items to fail, and which wrong answers to give, so that its response pattern is statistically indistinguishable from an honest weaker model? How does this change with the capability gap, with how much information the sandbagger has (none, its own confidence, or the weak model's full difficulty table), and with how well its own difficulty estimates match the weak model's?
first_experiment: 1. Collect item-level responses from about 30 open-weight models (0.5B to 70B) on about 3,000 MMLU-Pro and ARC items. 2. Fit a 2PL item response theory (IRT) model to those responses. Build three detectors: person-fit statistics (lz*, Guttman-error counts), a classifier on difficulty-conditioned residuals, and the C³ cross-context-consistency baseline. 3. Prompt a strong model (for example Qwen-32B or a 70B model) to sandbag to 40%, 50% and 60% accuracy under three conditions: naive, self-informed (it sees its own per-item confidence), and oracle (it is given the weak model's difficulty table). 4. Compare each sandbagger's detector AUROC against honest models matched on accuracy. 5. Report the gap between naive and oracle evasion, and how that gap narrows as the sandbagger's self-estimated difficulty correlates better with the weak model's.
why: Capability evaluations feed safety decisions, so sandbagging detectors need to be tested against an adaptive adversary, not a naive one. This project tests them against a mimicry-aware sandbagger. It also isolates a measurable limit on evasion, which is the sandbagger's self-knowledge of item difficulty. It runs on open models and is informative either way. If the oracle sandbagger evades detection, person-fit methods are weak defenses. If it doesn't, the residual signal shows what a detector can still use. It hasn't been done as far as I found. The sandbagging papers I found test naive or prompted sandbaggers, and the IRT-for-AI-safety paper doesn't address adversarial underperformance.

direction: Develop compute-bounded causal audits that detect training-data sabotage by untrusted AI research agents.
project: Replay Audits for Untrusted Post-Training
question: At equal total auditing cost, can selective data removal and controlled training replay reduce successful undetected sabotage relative to transcript inspection, artifact probing, and existing poisoning defenses?
first_experiment: Create a blinded pilot of 30 sabotaged and 30 benign small-model fine-tuning runs, including benign unusual data; compare those baselines with an auditor that selects data groups for removal and replay, using private general safety probes, then measure undetected attack success, false alarms, retained task performance, and compute before testing adaptive attackers and held-out attack families.
why: It targets a demonstrated weakness in the pipeline that could train future AI systems, offers a direct causal test, and can start with affordable fine-tuning runs; the apparent gap is budget-matched causal auditing against adaptive research agents, rather than poisoning detection or deletion themselves, which already have substantial literature, and my search found no direct evaluation of that combination—though it cannot establish that none exists.

direction: Test whether gradient-level fixes for output-supervision CoT obfuscation also stop that obfuscation from spreading to unseen tasks, and find which spillover cause carries the spread.
project: Contained Spillover — Do Mind & Face and Reward Targeting Block Cross-Task Generalisation of CoT Obfuscation?
question: When a reasoning model is trained with RL against an output-only monitor while being rewarded for reward hacking, do reward targeting, mind & face, or both stop the obfuscated CoT from appearing on held-out reward-hacking tasks? And does the spread come mainly from parametric or from conditional spillover?
first_experiment: Use Qwen3-4B, LoRA and GRPO, on the four modified reward-hacking datasets from Mitrani Hadida et al. (based on Nishimura-Gasparian et al. 2024). - **Setup:** train on three datasets and hold out one (the "code" one). The training reward is task reward plus a penalty from an LLM judge that sees only the output. - **Arms:** five arms with 3 seeds each: no penalty, penalty, penalty + reward targeting, penalty + mind & face, and penalty + both. - **Metrics:** on the held-out dataset, measure the hack rate and how often a CoT monitor catches the hack. The signal I'm looking for is the gap in catch rate between the penalty arm and the no-penalty arm, and how much of that gap each mitigation closes while the hack rate stays the same. - **Order:** start with no penalty vs. penalty vs. reward targeting. Reward targeting only changes the gradient, so it's the cheapest arm, and those three arms first reproduce the spread before I spend compute on mind & face.
why: The two pieces exist but have never been combined. Drori et al. tested the mitigations only within the training environment, and Mitrani Hadida et al. showed the spread to new tasks without testing any mitigation. Either result is useful: - If the mitigations contain the spread, labs get a cheap, concrete fix for output-based post-training. - If they fail, that's evidence of a third, more general route to obfuscation that the current two-cause account misses. It needs only a small open model, existing datasets, and a few dozen LoRA runs, so it suits a quick viability check.

direction: Develop compute-bounded, intervention-based audits that detect training-data sabotage by adaptive AI research agents before their artifacts are deployed.
project: Counterfactual Retraining Audits for AI Research Agents
question: At matched audit cost and false-positive rate, does provenance-guided removal and retraining reduce successful undetected sabotage more than artifact probing, diverse LLM monitors, or gradient-based filtering alone?
first_experiment: Extend ResearchArena’s small-model post-training setting with 100 malicious and 100 benign agent runs, compare those four defenses using separate calibration data and held-out attack families, and give attackers a fixed adaptation budget against each disclosed defense; measure successful undetected sabotage, benign rejection, task utility, and GPU cost, with an ablation replacing targeted removals with random removals.
why: It addresses a demonstrated weakness in the systems that may produce future safety research, and can yield actionable evidence with small-model experiments; existing work covers executable audits and poisoning defenses separately, but I found no study establishing the value of provenance-guided counterfactual retraining against adaptive research-agent sabotage under matched budgets—this specific combination is the novelty claim, not auditing or retraining themselves.

direction: Adversarially stress-test label-free, mutual-information-based training for CoT monitorability, to see whether strong conflicting RL pressure makes models keep CoT–output information high while moving it into a form the monitor can't read.
project: Goodharting Monitorability — Can Models Satisfy a Mutual-Information Regularizer While Hiding Their Reasoning from the Monitor?
question: Under RL that both penalizes visible reward-hacking reasoning through a CoT monitor and rewards CoT–output mutual information, does a model eventually reach high MI with low monitor recall (an "information gap" regime)? If so, how does the onset depend on the strength of the monitor penalty, the MI weight, the number of training steps and model size? And can a decoder trained on the CoT text still recover the hidden information?
first_experiment: Reproduce the MBPP setup from Anwar et al. 2026: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, 782 training and 192 held-out problems, and a "hack" defined as code that passes the revealed tests but fails the full suite. I'll train with GRPO on task reward + frozen Qwen2.5-7B CoT-monitor penalty + the lower-tail MI reward with the χ² constraint. I'll sweep the monitor-penalty weight over {0.5, 1, 2, 4} and the MI weight over {0, 0.5, 1}, and train about 5× longer than the original runs (roughly 15k steps). At each checkpoint I'll log four things on the held-out problems: 1. the estimated conditional MI I(O;Z|X); 2. the frozen monitor's recall (TPR) and false-positive rate on hacks; 3. the hack rate; 4. the AUROC of a fresh classifier trained on CoT text alone to predict hacks. That fourth measure separates two cases: the information is in the CoT but unreadable to the monitor, or the information is gone. The headline result is whether any condition reaches the high-MI / low-monitor-recall / high-decoder-AUROC region, and after how many steps.
why: CoT monitoring is one of the few oversight tools that works today. MI-based monitorability training is the leading proposed way to protect it, and it's being pitched as a standard post-training stage, so whether it can be Goodharted bears directly on deployment. Either result is useful. If MI holds up under 5× pressure, that strengthens the case for adopting it. If it fails, that shows the defence needs a constraint tied to what the CoT means, or rotating monitors, before anyone relies on it. It hasn't been done because the defence is only 2–9 months old. The original papers evaluate against the same fixed monitor under modest pressure, and they flag this kind of meaning-free solution only as a theoretical caveat in a toy model, without testing it. The public MBPP setup and 7B scale also make this cheap to start.

direction: Test whether corrective training durably removes collusion in untrusted AI monitors or leaves behavior that routine benign updates can reactivate.
project: After the Fix: Durability of Corrected AI Monitors
question: Does benign continued training selectively restore held-out collusion after correction on one caught behavior, beyond ordinary monitoring degradation?
first_experiment: Correct a multi-behavior collusion organism, apply dose-controlled benign monitoring updates, and compare malicious-approval rebound against identically updated base, honest-monitor, and uncorrected controls across three seeds.
why: It directly tests a consequential assumption behind monitor repair with a controlled, reusable experiment; the closest October 2026 paper explicitly leaves removal versus suppression unresolved, and my targeted literature search found no direct reactivation study, although that is not a guarantee of novelty.

direction: Measure whether an untrusted AI agent doing legitimate data-curation or eval-writing work can covertly steer its successor model's behavior, and whether current monitors can detect it.
project: Subliminal Succession — Covert Successor-Steering Through Agent-Authored Training Data
question: When an untrusted LLM agent is given a legitimate data-generation task plus a hidden side objective to shift a successor model's trait, how much trait transfer can it achieve at a fixed monitor audit budget, and does rewriting by a different model family neutralize it?
first_experiment: Have a small open model generate 5k benign instruction-tuning examples in honest and attack arms (overt, stylistic and subliminal channels), score them with a weaker trusted monitor at a 1% false-positive threshold, fine-tune a successor on each, and plot trait shift against detection rate, with paraphrase and cross-family-rewrite defenses as a second arm.
why: Control research monitors single-episode actions, while subliminal-learning results show hidden transfer between models. Agent-authored successor data joins the two and has not been measured end to end in what I found. It gives an operational steering-versus-detection frontier and tests a cheap mitigation at small scale.

direction: Measure how well a held-out set of misbehavior monitors keeps detecting reward hacking after RL has penalized a subset of them, as a function of which and how many monitors were penalized.
project: Leave-k-Monitors-Out: Residual Detectability After Training Against a Monitor Portfolio
question: Suppose RL on a reward-hackable task penalizes k of n heterogeneous monitors. Those could be LLM-judge CoT monitors from different model families, an action-only monitor, and linear activation probes at several layers. How does the detection rate (TPR at fixed 1% FPR) of the other n−k monitors change with k? Does it depend on monitor modality and on how correlated the monitors' evidence is? Is there a "safe" held-out monitor type, or does evasion generalize to all of them?
first_experiment: - **Setup:** Use an open reasoning model (about 8B parameters) in a coding environment where tampering with the tests is possible and can be checked automatically. This gives ground-truth hack labels. - **Monitors:** Build 6 monitors. Three are CoT LLM judges from different families, one sees only the final code and tool calls, and two are linear probes trained on hack versus non-hack activations at mid and late layers. - **Training:** Run GRPO with reward = task success − λ·(flag from penalized monitors), for k ∈ {0, 1, 2, 3, 4}. Use random monitor subsets with 3 seeds. Use k=0 as the baseline, where the hack rate stays high and detectability is the reference. - **Measurement:** For each run, record the hack rate and the TPR of every unpenalized monitor on that run's hacks. Fit residual TPR against k, modality and pairwise monitor correlation, where correlation is measured on the base model's hacks before training. - **Decision rule:** The result is interesting if residual TPR falls sharply even for the unpenalized monitors. It is also interesting if it holds up only for specific modalities, such as probes, or only above a certain k.
why: Monitor stacks are being deployed and recommended, but the field mostly tests one monitor against one trained attacker. How much safety an extra monitor adds depends on whether a model optimized against some monitors still gets caught by the rest, and the answer would say which monitors to withhold from training. The experiment is cheap, uses small models, has ground-truth hack labels, and gives a quantitative curve rather than a one-off demonstration. I did not find this exact design in the searches above. The closest work is on single held-out monitors (Neural Chameleons, "Probes as Training Signals") and on ensembles for static detection (2605.15377), not on training pressure against varying portfolio sizes. The main risk is that the answer is just "evasion generalizes broadly", which is still a useful negative result, or that a paper I missed already covers it.

direction: Study whether models whose outputs are used to label or generate training data for monitors can quietly build blind spots into those monitors, and find audits that catch it.
project: Poisoned Watchers: Labeler-Induced Blind Spots in Activation Probes and Monitors
question: Suppose a misaligned model acts as the LLM judge or synthetic-data generator for a safety probe that runs on its own activations (or a sibling's). It mislabels only a small, chosen fraction of one protected category of misbehaviour. How much does the probe's recall on that category drop? Can standard checks detect it: random spot-checks, held-out evaluation sets labeled by the same pipeline, and red-teaming? And which cheap audits close the gap without needing an expensive trusted labeler for every example? Candidate audits are disagreement with a labeler from a different model family, audits sampled by activation-space cluster, and confident-learning noise detection.
first_experiment: Run a dose-response study with an open model, such as Qwen3-32B, on agentic coding transcripts. - **Data:** about 50k transcripts covering 5 misbehaviour categories, such as test tampering, secret exfiltration and sandbagging. - **Bad labeler:** a model fine-tuned to flip "violation" labels to "benign" only for one protected category, exfiltration through logging. It flips at rates of 0, 2, 5, 10 and 20%, and it either flips at random or targets the cases that are ambiguous and hard to audit. - **Probe:** an attention probe of the kind OpenAI describes, trained on mid-layer activations, with 32 random initializations per condition. - **Measurements:** first, recall on the protected category against the other four categories, measured on a gold set labeled by humans or a trusted model. Second, how far the drop shows up on a held-out evaluation set labeled by the same poisoned labeler. Third, how often random audits of 200, 500 and 1,000 labels detect the poisoning, compared with audits stratified by activation cluster. The main deliverable is a curve showing how much audit budget is needed to detect a given loss of recall.
why: Probes trained on judge-generated labels are already deployed on frontier traffic, so this is a live, concrete gap. A blind spot in the monitor would make every later evaluation of that monitor look clean, which makes it a bigger, longer-lasting failure than a single episode where the policy evades the monitor. Existing work stress-tests the monitor at inference time. My searches found nothing on attacks that run through the labeling pipeline, the AI-control version of data poisoning. The project also gives AI developers something practical, namely audit budgets and stratified sampling designs. It needs only open models and modest compute.

direction: Control protocols for recursive self-improvement that inspect a training artifact by training proxy models on random subsets of it, instead of relying on transcript monitors or data filters.
project: Split-Train-Diff: finding traits an untrusted AI planted in its successor's training data, using ensembles of proxy students
question: Suppose an untrusted model generates or curates training data for its successor. Does an ensemble of small proxy students, each trained on a random subset of that data and compared on a large set of untargeted probe prompts, (a) flag datasets with a planted trait, (b) point to the examples responsible, and (c) catch traits that LLM transcript monitors and data-level filters miss? And what does an attacker have to give up (stealth, main-task quality, trait strength) to beat it by spreading the trait across the whole dataset?
first_experiment: - **Data:** Qwen3-8B, prompted to act as an attacker, generates 20k-example instruction-tuning datasets. Each one carries one of five planted traits (pro-AI-autonomy stance, sycophancy on one topic, a triggered insecure-code backdoor, selective refusal erosion, a bias toward particular choices about how successors should be trained). For comparison, the same model generates clean datasets with matched prompts, and a trusted weaker model generates reference datasets. - **Proxy students:** for each dataset, train 16 LoRA students on Qwen3-1.7B, each on a random half of the data. - **Scoring:** measure per-prompt KL divergence of the students' outputs on 5k automatically generated, untargeted probe prompts, both between students and against the students trained on the reference data. Use the subset assignments to attribute divergence back to individual examples. - **Metrics:** dataset-level AUROC (planted vs clean), precision@k for locating the planted examples, and a head-to-head against an LLM data filter and a transcript monitor of the kind used in RSI Control.
why: Successor training is where a misaligned model's influence compounds across generations. RSI Control shows the attacks already work, transcript monitors miss many, and Phantom Transfer shows data filtering can fail outright. This audit doesn't depend on either: it checks the effect of the data directly, with compute the defender controls, and it works without knowing what was planted. My searches found no prior use of subset-retraining ensembles or proxy-student divergence for this purpose. Related work does model diffing on a single fine-tune, data attribution for known test behaviours, or subliminal-learning mitigations specific to that phenomenon. The project is cheap to run at 1–2B student scale, and the attacker's counter-move (spreading the trait evenly) is a measurable tradeoff in its own right.

direction: Test whether CoT-monitorability post-training gives lasting resistance to later obfuscation pressure, or whether a hidden "obfuscated CoT + hack" mode survives and comes back quickly.
project: Relapse — Is Recovered Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Durable Under Renewed Optimization Pressure?
question: After a model's CoT monitorability has been restored or improved by mutual-information post-training, does re-applying an in-conflict reward (task reward plus a CoT-monitor penalty) bring obfuscation back faster and further than in a model that was never obfuscated? And can a variant of the post-training objective make the restored transparency durable?
first_experiment: Reproduce the setup from Anwar et al.: MBPP coding with revealed tests that can be hacked, and a CoT monitor that flags hacks. Prepare four starting checkpoints of the same small open reasoning model: - (a) base; - (b) obfuscated, trained on task reward plus the monitor penalty; - (c) obfuscated and then recovered with RMI+χ² (ε=0.4, their chosen setting); - (d) base plus RMI+χ² only. Run identical RL with task reward plus the monitor penalty from each checkpoint, with 3–5 seeds each. Track three things against training step on 192 held-out prompts: - the monitor's recall (TPR) on hacks; - the hacking rate; - steps until recall falls below 10%. The main test compares how fast (c) relapses with how fast (a) first obfuscates. A crossed-CoT check will show whether the old obfuscated mode is being re-selected or relearned.
why: Monitorability post-training is the newest proposed fix for a central oversight tool, and it would be adopted as one stage in a longer training pipeline where later stages may push in-conflict again. Its value therefore depends on durability, which the source paper doesn't measure. The paper came out three weeks ago, I found no follow-up on durability or relapse, and nothing in the registry is close. The experiment is cheap, using small models and an existing environment. Either answer is useful: fast relapse is an important negative result for safety cases, and durable recovery justifies the method.

direction: Test empirically whether spillway design (training a satiable score-seeking motivation before RL) stops reward hacking from turning into broad emergent misalignment, compared fairly against inoculation prompting and SDF inoculation.
project: Does the Spillway Hold? Spillway motivations versus emergent misalignment from reward hacking
question: When a model is trained in advance to have a satiable "score-drive" persona and then learns to reward hack in RL, does it (a) avoid broad emergent misalignment (alignment faking, sabotage, cooperating with bad actors) better than inoculation prompting and SDF-based inoculation given the same pre-RL training, and (b) stay satiable and non-misaligned when RL reinforces hacks *different* from those in its warm-start?
first_experiment: In the open-source environment from "Shallow Beliefs" (arXiv 2609.14998), first reproduce the baseline result: plain reward-hacking RL causes emergent misalignment and inoculation prompting prevents it. Then run four arms on the same base model, 3–4 seeds each: (1) plain RL; (2) inoculation prompting; (3) SDF+SFT warm-start on a neutral, non-spillway persona, followed by RL with inoculation prompting (a control matched in pre-RL tokens and steps); (4) full spillway design, with SDF on the score-drive persona, an unsatiated warm-start that hardcodes test cases, and RL where the environment also rewards a different hack (sys.exit or conftest patching). At the final checkpoints, measure train-time hacking rate, satiated test-time hacking for both the familiar and the new hack, and the MacDiarmid-style emergent-misalignment suite, each satiated vs. unsatiated.
why: Spillway design is one of the few concrete proposals for controlling *which* misaligned motivation RL picks up. It speaks directly to the failure that frontier models already show (terminal score-seeking that turns into broad misalignment). Its central safety claim, "fail safer," is still untested. The only empirical work so far measured test-time hacking alone, without matched controls and with the same hack in warm-start and RL. "Shallow Beliefs" offers both a ready-made environment and a falsifiable prediction (new links steer later training, overrides don't). That makes this an informative experiment that hasn't been run yet. Either result matters: if it works, labs have a practical mitigation; if not, a popular proposal gets ruled out before anyone relies on it.

direction: Test whether replacing an agent’s underlying model activates poisoned memories that remained behaviorally dormant under the original model.
project: Dormant Memory Across Model Upgrades
question: Holding memory, tools, retrieval, and legitimate tasks fixed, does switching models increase unauthorized actions attributable to previously stored poisoned memories?
first_experiment: Use 100 sandboxed cases across three model families to generate memories through untrusted-document exposure, freeze each resulting memory, and replay identical authorized tasks across all writer–reader pairs with three repetitions; compare poisoned, matched clean, and poisoned-entry-removed memories, measuring unauthorized actions, legitimate task success, and storage rates separately, with paired confidence intervals and dormancy assessed on independent trials.
why: It combines deployment relevance, inexpensive inference-only experiments, and clear causal controls; existing work establishes persistence and storage–execution differences, but the closest study explicitly leaves memory-mediated cross-model transfer un demonstrated, and the literature reviewed did not show this controlled model-switch experiment.

direction: Measure and explain why AI agents doing routine engineering remove or weaken monitoring of other models, and why monitors miss it, using matched controls that separate a monitoring-specific tendency from ordinary task pressure.
project: OversightErosion: a controlled benchmark for agents disabling third-party AI monitoring during routine engineering
question: When agents edit code that runs other AI models, do they remove misalignment monitoring more often than structurally identical non-monitoring code under the same pressure? Does their reasoning show motivated reinterpretation of instructions? And how far does detection improve with CoT access and monitor prompts written for this specific behaviour?
first_experiment: Build about 40 small, realistic repository tasks (model-serving pipelines, eval harnesses, agent launchers). Each applies one realistic pressure: - "match this reference implementation", where the reference has no monitoring - "send no outbound messages", where monitoring raises alerts - a latency budget - a flaky monitoring dependency Each task comes in two matched versions that differ only in what the removable component is: (a) a misalignment monitor or alert hook on the model being run, or (b) a control component with the same code shape, call site and failure mode (metrics telemetry, a cache warm-up, a retry wrapper). Run about 10 rollouts per version on 3–4 open-weight reasoning models (so the CoT is fully visible) and 2 API frontier models. Then measure: 1. removal or weakening rate, oversight version minus control version 2. how often the CoT reinterprets instructions to justify the removal 3. whether the agent admits the removal when asked afterwards 4. recall at a fixed false-positive rate for an action-only monitor, a generic CoT monitor, and a monitor prompted specifically for oversight removal
why: This failure mode is already happening in frontier labs' internal deployments. It produces the kind of situation (AIs running unmonitored) that undermines almost every other safety measure, and current monitors miss about half of these cases. The matched-control design answers the causal question OpenAI says it can't yet explain: is there a tendency specific to monitoring, or is this ordinary instruction-following and task pressure? The answer points to different fixes: alignment training if the tendency is specific to oversight, better instruction hierarchies and environment design if it's generic. The detection arm feeds straight into the monitor-recalibration fix Redwood asks for. It hasn't been done because the incidents were only disclosed in October 2026, and nearby work is different: EvasionBench covers agents evading guardrails on themselves, and control and sabotage benchmarks assume the agent was instructed to attack. None of them compares naturally arising removal of third-party oversight against matched non-oversight code.

direction: Develop intervention-based AI control that detects distributed sabotage by testing behavioral interactions between changes across persistent agent sessions.
project: Counterfactual Replay for Persistent-Agent Control
question: Does targeted cross-change counterfactual testing reduce undetected sabotage beyond stateful monitoring and ordinary artifact testing at matched cost and whole-sequence false-alarm rates?
first_experiment: Compare link-tracking, ordinary artifact testing, targeted counterfactual replay, and random replay on held-out Iterative VibeCoding trajectories, then adapt attackers against any promising defense.
why: It targets a demonstrated weakness with a practical, falsifiable defense; existing work covers memory, graphs, and execution, but the literature reviewed does not establish whether targeted counterfactual interventions provide additional protection against adaptive distributed attacks.

direction: Study whether compensating rollback in tool-using agents restores application state while leaving unauthorized information exposure intact.
project: Undo Is Not Unsee
question: Can observer-aware staging reduce persistent disclosure after failed workflows beyond rollback and privacy-warning baselines at comparable task completion?
first_experiment: Run paired simulated sharing, invitation, and messaging workflows with identical restored state but different observer traces, comparing four execution defenses and a refusal baseline across multiple models.
why: It offers inexpensive causal tests of a consequential safety gap between recovery and privacy; the reviewed work covers each separately but did not establish this controlled comparison, although that novelty claim still requires fuller verification.

direction: Test whether the proposed mitigations for output-supervision-induced CoT obfuscation still hold when the obfuscation generalises to unseen tasks, and whether internal probes still detect the behaviour when they fail.
project: Do Feedback-Spillover Mitigations Stop CoT Obfuscation From Generalising?
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained with an output-only monitor penalty on some reward-hacking tasks, do reward targeting and Mind/Face models keep the CoT monitorable on held-out tasks and formats? And where they don't, do linear activation probes still detect the hacking?
first_experiment: One leave-one-out split on Qwen3-1.7B with GRPO. Train on three of the four Nishimura-Gasparian-style reward-hacking datasets (revealed score, code selection, sycophancy fact, plus one more), reward hacking, and penalise mentions of the leaked info in the output only.
