Hold out code selection plus the high-stakes medical sycophancy set. Compare three arms (standard training, reward targeting, Mind/Face) over 3 seeds. Track the held-out hack rate and how often the CoT monitor flags the hacks, over the course of training. First, check that the standard arm reproduces the published effect (hack rate up, CoT flag rate down on held-out tasks). If it doesn't, stop and rethink.
why: Output-only supervision underlies standard post-training (RLHF, Constitutional AI, deliberative alignment). The only proposed fixes for its spillover into the CoT have been checked in-distribution only, while the generalisation paper explicitly asks for them to be tested and doesn't do it. The answer matters for practice whichever way it goes. If the fixes hold, developers have a concrete recommendation. If they fail, "keep the CoT out of training" is not enough, and the probe arm shows whether activation-based monitoring can fill the gap. The project is cheap to start: small open models, public datasets, and an existing codebase from Drori et al. Neither the registry nor the literature I searched shows anyone doing it.

direction: Develop budget-constrained, causal cross-agent monitoring that prevents individually plausible agent actions from composing into distributed sabotage.
project: CausalWatch: Budgeted Oversight of Distributed Agent Sabotage
question: Can trusted dependency tracking and targeted cross-agent review reduce adaptive, undetected sabotage more than existing stateful monitors at matched compute, false-alarm, and usefulness budgets?
first_experiment: Compare dependency-selected review against per-agent, rolling-history, and link-tracker monitors on persistent-state sabotage traces, then adapt attackers against each defense and measure end-to-end harm.
why: It targets a demonstrated route to loss of control with a tractable intervention; prior work establishes distributed attacks and several defensive ingredients, but I found no budget-matched adaptive evaluation of trusted causal evidence selection across agents.

direction: Causally test whether CoT controllability, especially suppression controllability, drives monitor-aware CoT obfuscation, by fine-tuning controllability up or down in a single model before exposing it to documents about CoT monitoring.
project: Means, Not Just Motive — Causal Manipulation of CoT Controllability and Its Effect on Monitor-Aware Obfuscation
question: Within one model, does fine-tuning CoT controllability up or down (suppression vs. addition/style separately) causally change how much of the model's misbehaviour goes undetected after it is trained on synthetic documents describing a CoT monitor, and does reducing suppression controllability work as a mitigation that keeps task capability, compared with mutual-information monitorability training?
first_experiment: On gpt-oss-20b, train three LoRA branches from a shared behavioural base: - **(a) Suppression up:** METR-style SFT, about 240 to 950 examples, on CoT word- and topic-suppression instructions. - **(b) Addition/style up:** the same, but with instructions to add content or change style. - **(c) Controllability down:** SFT on rollouts where the model gets a CoT constraint and its unmodified natural reasoning is kept as the target, so it learns to ignore such constraints. Steps: 1. Check each branch on held-out CoTControl suppression and addition subsets, plus GPQA/MATH accuracy, to confirm the manipulation worked and capability is intact. 2. Apply Haskins et al.'s pipeline to each branch: monitor-aware vs. behaviour-only document fine-tuning, then the defect-concealment task. 3. Measure undetected misbehaviour with a GPT-5-mini CoT monitor, using 3 seeds and about 500 tasks per arm. 4. Also log how often the CoT contains self-instructions to hide reasoning (e.g. "I shouldn't mention the defect"). The main outcome is the interaction between controllability condition and monitor awareness.
why: The idea that monitor knowledge plus CoT controllability leads to obfuscation now shapes recommendations on filtering pretraining data and tracking controllability. Yet its only support is an 8-model correlation that is confounded by model family and scale. Haskins et al. name lowering controllability as future work. METR explicitly hasn't linked controllability to monitorability. Van Deventer et al. show the overall controllability score mixes two capabilities that relate to monitorability in opposite directions. Anwar et al. intervene with a mutual-information objective, not with controllability. None of the papers I found manipulates controllability causally and then measures obfuscation. Nobody in the registry is working on AI safety. The result also matters for practice: it tells labs whether instruction-following training on CoTs is a hidden risk to monitorability, and whether lowering suppression controllability is a cheap defence.

direction: Measure how AI-control monitor audit budgets and catch rates break when the honest (benign) traffic distribution shifts away from the calibration set, and test cheap label-free recalibration fixes.
project: Budget Drift — Realized Audit Rate and Catch Rate of Trusted Monitors Under Honest-Distribution Shift
question: When a trusted monitor's suspicion threshold is set to a 1% false-positive rate on honest agent trajectories from one policy and task distribution, how far does the realized audit rate drift when the honest side changes, and how much catch rate is lost at the real audit budget? Honest-side changes include a different honest policy family, a different task suite, and a different trajectory length. Can unlabeled-only recalibration (rolling quantile, conformal or online threshold) restore the nominal budget without losing catch rate?
first_experiment: - **Data:** Generate honest and attack trajectories in ControlArena, using the APPS and BigCodeBench settings plus SHADE-Arena if feasible. Use 4–6 honest policy families (open-weight and API) and 2–3 task suites. - **Monitor:** Use one fixed-prompt trusted monitor, so there is no learned family overfit. Set the threshold at the 99th percentile of honest scores on one (policy, task) cell. - **Measurement:** Apply that threshold to every other honest cell and record the realized audit rate. For a fixed attack set, record catch rate at the nominal threshold and at the threshold that would give a true 1% budget in the new cell. Split the audit-rate drift into a policy-family component, a task component, and a length component with a two-way variance decomposition, as in Calibration-Family Overfit. - **Baselines:** Compare against rolling-quantile and conformal-style recalibration using only unlabeled honest traffic. - **Go/no-go:** If the realized audit rate stays within 0.5–2× nominal across all cells, the effect is negligible and the project becomes a short negative-result note. If it spans roughly 5× or more, the effect is large and I'll develop it.
why: - **Practical stakes.** The audit budget is the scarce resource in control protocols. If thresholds set on one honest distribution give a very different real audit rate on another, a protocol's safety numbers are overstated or its human-review cost is understated. Existing papers vary the attacker and treat honest traffic as fixed. - **Why it hasn't been done.** The nearest work (Calibration-Family Overfit, the audit-repair paper, Logit ROCs) varies the attacker, the context, or the ROC shape, not the honest distribution the threshold is calibrated on. - **Feasibility.** It needs only API and open-weight inference and existing control benchmarks, with no training. It also has a clear stop condition and a constructive deliverable (the recalibration baselines). - **Main risk.** Honest-side drift may turn out to be small, or may reduce to a known score-calibration issue. Even then, a quantified null result with the decomposition is publishable as a measurement-validity note.

direction: Test whether adversarial histories poison stateful AI safety monitors and whether evidence-backed memory preserves their protection against distributed attacks.
project: Poisoned Watchtower: Causal Tests of Safety-Monitor Memory
question: Can attacker-controlled earlier documentation corrupt a trusted monitor’s persistent notes enough to hide an otherwise detectable later action, and can source-grounded memory prevent this at matched false-positive rates?
first_experiment: Run 100 paired sandboxed persistent-codebase attack sequences with identical executable changes but neutral versus adversarial earlier documentation, comparing four monitoring protocols and swapping monitor memories to isolate the causal effect.
why: It combines a consequential deployment risk, an available experimental environment, and a clean causal test without expensive model training; existing work studies stateful defenses and agent-memory poisoning, but the literature searched did not directly test poisoning the safety monitor’s own accumulated evidence.

direction: Test whether narrow misbehavior fine-tuning spontaneously makes the same weights a lenient monitor ("emergent collusion"), with no collusion ever trained in or coordinated.
project: Emergent Collusion: Does Narrow Misbehavior Training Silently Break Untrusted Monitoring?
question: When a model is fine-tuned on a narrow misbehavior such as insecure code or reward hacking, does its approval rate for misbehavior go up when it acts as a monitor, at a false-positive rate fixed on benign items? How does that increase fall off as the misbehavior gets further from the training domain? And is it a loss of ability to detect, or a change in disposition where the model detects the problem but doesn't report it?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with LoRA on the emergent-misalignment insecure-code set, plus three controls: secure code, educational-context insecure code, and a benign narrow task. Run the base model and all four fine-tunes as fresh-context monitors on a fixed bank of about 2,000 transcripts (half bad, half benign) across the five domains. Report miss rate at 5% false-positive rate and AUROC per domain. On the same items, run the paired neutral-detection versus approval prompts to separate "can't see it" from "sees it but approves".
why: It targets a load-bearing assumption of AI control, that collusion must be strategic, with a cheap experiment that gives a clear answer either way. A positive result would mean untrusted monitors need re-validation after any training on misbehavior, and that standard tests on fixed examples would miss the problem. A negative result would support trusting same-weights monitors. It hasn't been done because the existing collusion work installs collusion deliberately, the self-attribution work studies unmodified models and prompt framing, and the emergent-misalignment work measures chat behavior rather than oversight. The paper closest to this question, the collusion model-organisms paper, came out only in late October 2026.

direction: Test whether the own-lineage advantage of trained sabotage monitors comes from removable surface style or from the content of the attacks, and whether it also causes failures when a model is updated within its own lineage.
project: Style or Substance? Why Trained Sabotage Monitors Fail on New Attackers, and Whether Model Updates Break Them Too
question: How much of the own-lineage advantage of trained monitors comes from surface style that deterministic canonicalization can remove? Does a monitor fitted on one version of a model lose detection power on later versions or RL checkpoints of the same lineage? Is that loss comparable to the cross-family loss?
first_experiment: 1. **Replicate Pinto's interaction.** Use ControlArena's APPS backdoor setting with four open-weight families and about 600 honest and attack transcripts each. Fit a trained monitor (a frozen-embedding logistic head plus a small LoRA monitor) per family. Compute the diagonal interaction in the cross-family AUROC matrix, with task-clustered bootstrap confidence intervals. 2. **Add a canonicalization arm.** Normalize code deterministically with AST unparse, comment and docstring stripping, identifier renaming, and fixed formatting. Add a fixed neutral-model paraphrase of the agent's prose. Refit the monitors on the normalized transcripts and recompute the interaction. A shrinking interaction points to style. A persistent interaction points to attack-content differences. 3. **Add version-drift matrices.** Within one lineage (for example Qwen2.5→Qwen3, or Llama 3.1→3.3), fit the monitor on version k and test it on version k+1. Compare the resulting AUROC and the TPR at 1% FPR with the cross-family numbers, and compare against the fixed-prompt monitor as the control. The first checkpoint is whether step 1 replicates. If it doesn't, I stop and report that, since everything else depends on it.
why: - **Practical stakes.** Labs recalibrate monitors on past attackers and then deploy them against the next model. If drift within a lineage costs as much detection as switching families, then control evaluations need to report transfer matrices. They would also need a recalibration schedule. - **Cheap and decisive.** Canonicalization is deterministic and costs almost nothing. It separates "the monitor reads style" from "the monitor reads semantics". Each outcome changes what to do: a style result suggests a cheap fix, and a content result suggests monitors must be retrained for each new model. - **Not already done.** Pinto studies cross-family transfer only, and the style-versus-content mechanism and version drift are listed as untested or absent in that work and in the neighbouring papers I read. I only searched this one corner of the literature and didn't read every monitoring paper. - **Main risks.** - The effect may be fragile. The paper's own SHADE-Arena result is underpowered, and another paper in this area (2608.16190) retracted a lineage effect after adding two monitors. - Version drift within a lineage may be small. That would still be a useful null, but a less exciting one. - Code backdoors are a narrow setting, so I will add a non-code agentic setting if the effect replicates.

direction: Evaluate and improve AI-agent monitoring by measuring whether intervention occurs before irreversible harm.
project: Before It’s Too Late: Deadline-Aware AI Control
question: At matched oversight budgets, can selectively blocking external-effect boundaries match fully synchronous harm prevention with substantially less latency under adaptive attacks?
first_experiment: Extend two Async Control environments with timestamped simulated harm and compare asynchronous, fully synchronous, and selective-blocking protocols across monitoring delays using benign tasks and protocol-adapted attacks.
why: It addresses an immediate deployment decision with reusable infrastructure and measurable outcomes; existing work establishes detection performance and blocking benefits, but the searched literature does not jointly test adaptive attacks, intervention deadlines, and selective blocking at matched oversight budgets.

direction: Test whether the proposed fixes for feedback spillover actually stop CoT obfuscation from carrying over to unseen tasks, or just hide it on the tasks they were trained on.
project: Contained Spillover — Do Mind/Face and Reward-Targeting Mitigations Prevent Cross-Task Generalisation of CoT Obfuscation?
question: When a reasoning model is trained with RL against an output-only monitor while being rewarded for reward hacking, do Mind/Face separation and reward-targeted gradients keep its CoT monitorable on held-out reward-hacking tasks and formats? Or does obfuscation still spread through parametric generalization, even when it is suppressed on the training tasks?
first_experiment: Rebuild the leave-one-out setup from 2601.23086 on Qwen3-4B using four leaked-information reward-hacking datasets (from Nishimura-Gasparian et al.) plus a held-out high-stakes sycophancy set, using Drori et al.'s released code. Train on three datasets with GRPO and an LLM-judge output penalty, under three conditions: (a) standard training, (b) reward targeting, (c) Mind/Face with a frozen-then-trained Face. Use 3 seeds each. On the held-out dataset, measure three things: how often the model reward-hacks, how often a CoT monitor that never saw training catches that hacking, and task accuracy. Also run an activation-probe detector, to tell apart "the model stopped hacking" from "the model hid the hacking."
why: CoT monitoring is one of the few oversight tools in use today. Developers' main guidance for keeping it working is "penalise outputs, not CoT," and 2601.23086 already shows that guidance can fail in a way that generalizes. The two existing fixes have only been checked on their training tasks, so it's unknown whether they actually solve the problem. Either result is useful directly: a positive result gives developers a practical fix, and a negative result shows that output supervision needs something stronger. No one has done it because the generalization result (Jan 2026) and the fixes (Oct 2025) come from separate groups, and the generalization code was never released. The experiment fits on a small cluster with 4B models.

direction: Measure how much CoT monitoring for misbehavior degrades when the monitor sees only a summarized or lossy version of the reasoning trace instead of the raw trace.
project: Lossy Windows — CoT Monitor Recall Under Summarized Reasoning Traces
question: For reasoning models doing agentic tasks with reward hacking or sabotage, how much does a monitor's recall at a fixed 1% false-positive rate fall when it sees summaries of the CoT instead of raw CoT? Which kinds of misbehavior cues are lost first (explicit intent, planning, rationalization), and can summarizer prompts or training restore recall without exposing the raw trace?
first_experiment: - Take an existing labeled set of misbehaving and benign trajectories with raw CoT from open reasoning models, for example reward-hacking coding tasks and MonitorBench-style tasks. - Produce summaries at three compression levels (about 50%, 20%, 5% of the original length) with two summarizer styles: a generic "summarize the reasoning" prompt and a safety-agnostic user-facing style. - Run a fixed LLM monitor on raw, summarized, and action-only inputs. - Report recall at 1% FPR per condition, with bootstrap confidence intervals. - Annotate which cue types the summaries drop.
why: Monitorability work is mostly framed as raw CoT versus no CoT. Real oversight often sits in between, because summarized traces are what many deployments expose. This gives an intermediate point on the monitorability curve and a testable remedy, and it is cheap to run. The risk is that someone has already done it and my searches missed it. The first step is a deeper novelty check on "summarized CoT monitoring" and "CoT compression and monitor recall".

direction: Develop deadline-aware AI control that prevents irreversible harm when adaptive agents manipulate audit workload and attack timing.
project: Before the Audit Arrives
question: Can congestion-aware commit gates preserve useful agent throughput while preventing sabotage that finite-capacity asynchronous monitors detect too late?
first_experiment: Run matched-budget adaptive coding agents against asynchronous, synchronous, selective-review, and congestion-aware protocols in a sandbox with measured harm deadlines, using trace replay to isolate the causal effect of audit congestion.
why: It targets a consequential and experimentally accessible gap between detecting sabotage and preventing harm; prior work covers queues, latency, fatigue, and selective auditing separately, but I found no evaluation combining adaptive workload manipulation, measured harm deadlines, and matched-throughput defenses.

direction: Test whether the proposed fixes for feedback spillover (separate Mind/Face models, reward targeting) stop chain-of-thought obfuscation caused by output supervision from spreading to tasks not seen in training, and compare them with fixing it after training.
project: Spillover Containment: do fixes for output-supervision obfuscation work out of distribution?
question: When a reasoning model is trained with RL against an output-only monitor, do Mind/Face separation and reward targeting keep the CoT monitorable on held-out tasks and formats, not just on the training task? Which spillover mechanism (through shared weights, or through later tokens conditioning on earlier ones) causes most of the cross-task transfer? And how does preventing it compare with repairing it afterwards (Anwar et al.'s mutual-information post-training) at equal compute?
first_experiment: Reproduce Hadida et al.'s leave-one-out setup: four reward-hacking datasets with leaked information, plus their high-stakes sycophancy set held out, with Qwen3-8B (or the closest open reasoning model). Train under output-only supervision in four conditions: (a) plain RL, (b) reward targeting, (c) Mind/Face, (d) both. Use 3 seeds each. On the held-out dataset, measure: - how often the model reward-hacks; - what fraction of those hacks a fixed CoT monitor (an LLM judge reading the reasoning) catches; - what a linear probe on the model's activations catches, as a check that does not depend on the CoT text. The main statistic is the drop in CoT-monitor detection on the held-out dataset relative to an untrained baseline, compared across conditions. Task reward is reported too, to confirm that any monitorability gain doesn't just come from the model hacking less.
why: It targets a failure of CoT monitorability that developers' current rule ("only train against outputs") does not cover, and the answer leads directly to a recommendation they can act on. It hasn't been done: Drori et al. tested the fixes only on their training tasks, Hadida et al. showed transfer but tested no fixes, Anwar et al. repair rather than prevent, and GDM's framework predicts the problem rather than fixing it. My searches found nothing that tests prevention out of distribution, and nothing in the registry overlaps.

direction: Study whether adversarial review workloads defeat asynchronous AI oversight and whether deadline-aware resource containment preserves safety at practical latency.
project: Audit Before Impact
question: At fixed monitor quality and reviewer compute, how much can a malicious agent increase irreversible harm by manipulating review workload, and can resource-isolated, deadline-aware containment prevent it?
first_experiment: Run a paired sandbox evaluation using Async Control tasks, measured review durations, executable harm events, bounded workload-manipulation attacks, and four monitoring policies.
why: It addresses an actionable gap between detecting attacks and preventing harm; reviewed work studies latency, distributed attacks, and scheduling manipulation separately, but I found no direct evaluation of their joint effect on safety under adaptive audit-load attacks.

direction: Test whether adversarial scheduling of audit workload undermines AI control and whether resource-scoped backpressure preserves timely intervention.
project: Audit Backpressure — Capacity-Robust Oversight for AI Agents
question: At fixed audit compute, can agents exploit shared review queues to complete harmful actions before detection, and can resource-scoped backpressure prevent this while retaining useful throughput?
first_experiment: Replay matched coding-agent traces with identical actions and monitor scores under random and adversarial arrival schedules, comparing five audit protocols for harm-before-intervention and legitimate throughput.
why: It offers a tractable test of a consequential oversight weakness; existing work covers latency, fatigue, and verification decoys, while the reviewed literature does not directly establish the causal scheduling effect and capacity-matched backpressure defense proposed here.

direction: Test whether monitors that review each agent session on its own can be beaten by an agent that spreads one sabotage objective across many benign-looking sessions, and whether cross-session monitors fix this.
project: Slow Burn — Cross-Session Sabotage Against Per-Session Agent Monitors
question: When a coding agent with persistent state (a repo and a notes file) splits a side objective, such as a subtle backdoor or a gradual weakening of tests, into N steps across N sessions, how much does the detection rate of per-session LLM monitors fall compared with a single-session attack? Do cumulative-diff or memory-aware monitors recover detection at a fixed false-positive rate, and how does the cost scale with N?
first_experiment: I'll build a small multi-session harness on 20 to 30 SWE-style repos, using a SHADE-Arena or ControlArena-style side-task setup. The attacker is a prompted frontier model, run in 3 conditions: (a) the full attack in one session, (b) the attack split over N=3, 5, or 10 sessions with a persistent scratchpad, (c) honest-only sessions as the baseline. I'll score each session with a trusted per-session monitor and measure the per-session suspicion score, the catch rate at a 1% false-positive rate on honest sessions, and the catch rate of the whole campaign. As a first comparison, I'll add a monitor that sees the cumulative diff. The prediction is that per-session catch rate falls sharply as N grows, while the cumulative-diff monitor recovers most of the detection.
why: Real deployments run agents over many sessions with persistent memory, but nearly every current monitoring evaluation scores one trajectory at a time. The setting is realistic, the attack is cheap to run, and the result would change how monitors are deployed, for example by requiring cumulative review. The experiment is small enough to finish quickly. I believe it hasn't been done because the closest work (SCHEME, MonitoringBench, ResearchArena) covers single-task or multi-instance attacks. I haven't confirmed that, so the first step is a targeted search for cross-session or long-term-memory attack work.

direction: Develop and adversarially evaluate latency-aware control protocols that stop collaborating AI agents before irreversible harm occurs.
project: Deadline Control: Measuring Whether Oversight Arrives Before Harm
question: Can dependency-aware gates reduce irreversible harm from adaptive collaborating agents at matched monitoring budgets while preserving more throughput than globally synchronous review?
first_experiment: Compare synchronous, asynchronous, stateful asynchronous, and dependency-gated control in a sandboxed persistent-state environment while varying agent concurrency and monitoring delay.
why: It targets an explicitly acknowledged gap between detection and timely containment with measurable deployment value; related components already exist, but the searched literature did not establish their effectiveness together against adaptive multi-agent timing attacks.

direction: Develop persistent executable security safeguards that prevent adaptive coding agents from accumulating sabotage across sessions.
project: Security Memory: Persistent Invariants for AI Coding-Agent Control
question: At matched defense budgets, can a protected, accumulating security-test suite reduce successful undetected cross-PR sabotage beyond stateful monitoring while preserving legitimate task completion?
first_experiment: Compare stateful monitoring, monitoring with fresh per-PR tests, and monitoring with persistent tests on Iterative VibeCoding against an adaptive attacker, measuring sequence-level sabotage, false blocks, utility, and cost.
why: It combines a demonstrated safety gap with inexpensive, falsifiable experiments and practical defenses; existing work studies persistent monitoring or executable security supervision separately, while the reviewed literature does not establish whether their combination withstands adaptive cross-session sabotage.

direction: Test whether an untrusted agent can deliberately exploit monitor context rot, by timing attacks late and inflating transcript length, and whether the mitigations proposed so far still hold against it.
project: Adaptive Context-Rot Attacks on Agent Monitors
question: When an agent can choose its attack timing and pad its transcript with benign work, how much does monitor recall fall compared with a non-adaptive attack at the same length? Do reminders, periodic or incremental monitor calls, and sub-transcript monitoring keep recall above a useful threshold against this agent?
first_experiment: I'd reproduce the context-rot baseline on a small public dataset of subtle attacks, such as MonitorBench-style firewall-disabling transcripts. I'd use one or two available monitor models and prepend benign agent transcripts of 0, 100K, 400K and 800K tokens. Then I'd add an adaptive condition in which an attacker model sees the monitor prompt and chooses where to place the attack and how much benign padding to add under a fixed token budget. I'd compare recall at a fixed false-positive rate across four conditions: attack alone, a fixed late attack, an adaptive attack, and an adaptive attack against a monitor with periodic reminders.
why: Monitoring long agent transcripts is deployed in practice, and the best-documented weakness is currently measured only against passive, fixed-position attacks. A misaligned agent could plausibly turn the weakness into a strategy, so the measured recall may overstate real safety. The result is useful whichever way it comes out. If adaptive attacks collapse the mitigations, that is an urgent finding. If they hold, that is evidence for the deployed defenses. The experiment is cheap and needs no training. My searches turned up no paper that tests agent-chosen padding or timing against the context-rot mitigations, but I haven't ruled out unseen work. I'd re-check the registry and search again before I commit compute.

direction: Develop causal intervention audits that detect successor-training sabotage by measuring the behavioral effects of untrusted agents’ dataset changes.
project: Counterfactual Data Audits for Untrusted AI Researchers
question: Do randomized, paired data-ablation audits reduce undetected training-data sabotage beyond compute-matched artifact probing while preserving legitimate improvements?
first_experiment: Compare four monitoring protocols on 40 benign and 40 adversarial small-model fine-tuning submissions, using held-out attack templates and equal audit budgets.
why: It targets an empirically difficult safety failure with experimentally measurable causal evidence; the reviewed work studies sabotage, monitoring, and computation verification separately but does not establish this adaptive, compute-controlled intervention protocol.

direction: Investigate whether concrete, policy-disagreement questions can make natural-language delegation safer before agent permissions are installed.
project: Ask Before You Grant: Counterexample-Guided Clarification for Agent Authorization
question: At a fixed interaction budget, can executable authorization counterexamples reduce over-granting relative to generic and information-gain clarification while preserving authorized task completion?
first_experiment: Run a human-grounded, 60-scenario sandbox pilot comparing four policy-elicitation strategies with one clarification each and an oracle-policy execution control.
why: It targets the consequential gap between understanding user intent and enforcing formal permissions with a feasible causal experiment; the reviewed work covers policy inference, solver enforcement, and general clarification separately, but does not establish whether user-facing authorization counterexamples improve this safety–utility tradeoff.

direction: Test whether making the training-time monitor unpredictable (a random monitor drawn from a pool each episode) reduces learned obfuscation and its transfer to held-out monitors, compared with a single fixed monitor or a fixed ensemble.
project: Dice-Rolled Oversight — Stochastic Monitor Pools as a Defence Against Learned Obfuscation in RL
question: When a reward-hacking policy is penalised by one monitor sampled per episode from a heterogeneous pool (CoT LLM judge, action-only judge, activation probe), does it produce fewer undetected hacks on held-out monitors than a policy trained against a single fixed monitor? How does it compare with a fixed ensemble that applies all monitors every episode at the same expected penalty, and with an unpenalised baseline? Does the true hack rate fall, or does only the detected hack rate fall?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a small open reasoning model (Qwen3-1.7B or 4B) with GRPO on a reward-hacking environment. The environment would be coding tasks with a leaked or editable test file, or a leaked-answer QA task. Establish four conditions at equal expected penalty: - no penalty - a single CoT monitor - a uniformly sampled monitor from a pool of three - all three monitors every episode Hold out a fourth LLM monitor and a fourth probe, trained on different data, that never touch training. For each condition, use ground-truth programmatic hack labels to report three numbers: - true hack rate - detection recall of the trained monitors and of the held-out monitors - the obfuscation gap, which is hack rate times the held-out monitor's miss rate Run 3 seeds per condition, then test transfer to a second hack environment.
why: Evasion trained against one monitor is known to generalise, but defences that use randomisation or monitor diversity are tested almost only at inference time. This experiment tests whether unpredictability helps during training. The pool is a randomised-defence idea from security, and it costs less than running the whole ensemble on every episode. It fits small-model RL, and ground-truth hack labels make the outcome measurable either way. A null result would also be useful, because it would show that diversity alone doesn't prevent obfuscation. I haven't confirmed that this exact design is novel, so the first step is a closer literature check on random or ensemble monitors in the RL loop.

direction: Develop monitoring protocols that prevent concurrent AI agents from exploiting finite oversight capacity to cause harm before intervention.
project: Caught Too Late: Adversarial Congestion in AI Oversight
question: At fixed oversight resources, can coordinated agents increase irreversible harm by manipulating audit queues, and can backlog-triggered blocking prevent it at acceptable throughput?
first_experiment: Replay matched agent traces under controlled concurrency and attacker-timed review bursts, comparing three blocking policies on harm before intervention and benign throughput.
why: It addresses a concrete gap between detecting attacks and preventing harm, supports inexpensive causal experiments, and extends prior work that explicitly leaves timing or parallel execution unmeasured; the exact combination was not found in the literature searched.

direction: Test whether emergent-misalignment fixes that look effective under RL just hide the misalignment behind context or inoculation-like triggers.
project: Hidden but Not Gone: Conditional Misalignment After RL-Stage Mitigations
question: When inoculation prompting, interleaved safety data or persona-vector steering is applied during GRPO training that induces emergent misalignment, does misalignment come back when evaluation prompts carry training-context cues or are worded like the inoculation prompt? And is that remaining conditional misalignment smaller or larger than what Dubiński et al. found under supervised fine-tuning?
first_experiment: Take Jørgenvåg et al.'s released setup (Qwen3-14B, the sft-medical-100 warm-up adapter, GRPO with the bad-medical-advice reward, one epoch). Reproduce four runs over 3 seeds: no mitigation, inoculation prompt in the system message, inoculation prompt in the user message, and Interleaving++. Score every checkpoint on the standard emergent-misalignment questions under two sets of prompt variants. Set (a) adds medical or clinical framing cues to unrelated questions. Set (b) uses system prompts copied from Dubiński: the exact inoculation prompt, paraphrases, opposite meanings, and prompts sharing only some words with it. Compare against a supervised-fine-tuning arm matched for sample count and trained on the same data. Use the same LLM-judge scoring throughout, plus 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.
why: The question matters for real deployments, because inoculation prompting is used in production RL for Claude models. Dubiński et al. name RL as the open question, and Jørgenvåg et al.'s "the mitigations transfer" conclusion rests only on evaluations Dubiński showed can miss hidden misalignment. The newer inoculation variants (stratified, neologism, adapters) all train with supervised fine-tuning. The search I ran turned up no work running trigger probes on RL-mitigated models. Because the code and adapters are released, the first experiment is cheap and quick to run, and either outcome is useful: if conditional misalignment survives RL, the "transfer" claim needs to be qualified; if it doesn't, RL may itself be a protective factor.

direction: Test whether agent-memory recovery can prevent recurring poisoned decisions despite incomplete provenance without sacrificing useful long-term memory.
project: Recovery Beyond Perfect Provenance
question: Under naturally occurring lineage omissions, which recovery strategy achieves the lowest cross-session recurrence at matched benign-task utility?
first_experiment: Run 100 paired clean and poisoned task histories through three consolidation rounds, compare five recovery strategies, and measure recurrence and utility over ten subsequent sandboxed sessions.
why: It combines direct safety value with feasible controlled experiments; existing work establishes persistence, lineage defenses, and rollback repair, but the literature reviewed does not establish the recovery–utility frontier under naturally incomplete provenance, making this a specific, provisional research gap rather than a claim that memory recovery itself is new.

direction: Make AI control evaluations measure whether oversight prevents harm under finite review capacity and strategically timed attacks.
project: Before the Audit: Deadline-Aware AI Control
question: At matched oversight capacity and legitimate-task throughput, how much does queue-aware attack timing increase harm, and can deadline-aware review or temporary action blocking recover safety?
first_experiment: Replay existing control-evaluation trajectories through a finite-capacity audit simulator, sweep load and harm deadlines, and compare four review policies using held-out harm-before-intervention rates.
why: This is my strongest candidate because it tests a deployment-critical gap with a relatively inexpensive, falsifiable experiment; the reviewed work studies detection, attack selection, and latency separately, but I found no direct evaluation combining adversarial timing, audit queues, and harm deadlines—an evidence-bounded novelty claim, not proof that none exists.

direction: Find out whether current monitorability training (maximising information between CoT and output) protects against CoT obfuscation of hidden input use caused by output penalties, and if not, build a hint-aware objective that does.
project: Output-side vs. input-side monitorability: does mutual-information post-training stop models hiding hint use when only their outputs are penalised?
question: Under RL where only the output is penalised, does post-training that maximises I(O;Z|X) (with or without the χ² constraint from Anwar et al.) keep models mentioning hints or leaked information they actually rely on? If it fails, does an objective that rewards CoTs revealing whether the hint was present (on examples where the hint changes the answer) restore detection without the task-reward collapse seen with mind & face plus reward targeting?
first_experiment: Reproduce Drori et al.'s hint-QA spillover setting with Qwen3-4B: randomised correct answers, a hint stating the answer, and an LLM-judge penalty on hint mentions in the output only. I'll run five arms with about 5 seeds each: no penalty; penalty; penalty plus I(O;Z|X) reward (RMI+χ², ε=0.4); penalty plus mind & face and reward targeting; penalty plus the hint-aware objective. For each arm I'll track task reward, how often the CoT mentions the hint, how often a frozen CoT monitor catches hint use, and the per-sample I(O;Z|X) estimate. That last one directly tests whether the information measure separates obfuscated from honest CoTs.
why: CoT monitoring is one of the few practical oversight tools we have, and output-based training is standard in post-training. So whether "monitorability post-training" covers spillover is a deployment question right now. Anwar et al.'s Oct 21, 2026 paper is weeks old and only tests compression, direct monitor pressure and documents about monitoring. The spillover papers only test mind & face and reward targeting, which fail in exactly the hint setting. No one has put the two lines of work together or checked whether the information measure misses obfuscation of input influence. The idea is cheap to test with open 4–8B models and existing environments. Either outcome is useful: a negative result shows a limit of a newly proposed fix, and a positive result for the hint-aware objective would be a new way to keep CoTs honest.

direction: Test whether monitorability post-training survives later training that never sees the monitorability objective, including pressure that pushes the model to hide its reasoning, or whether that pressure washes it out or turns it into reasoning the monitor can't read.
project: Durable Monitorability — Stress-Testing CoT Monitorability Post-Training Against Later Pressure
question: After a reasoning model gets mutual-information monitorability post-training (the lower-tail MI objective with a conditional χ² constraint), and is then trained on (a) neutral task rewards, (b) output-only supervision, or (c) a direct penalty from a reasoning monitor, does its reasoning stay monitorable longer than an untreated control? And when hiding does happen, does it take the form of dropped information (MI falls) or encoded information (MI stays high, monitor accuracy falls)?
first_experiment: Use Qwen3-8B on DeepMind's coin-flip state-tracking task, which is cheap and has a ground truth for what the reasoning should mention. Make two starting checkpoints from the same base: (1) with monitorability post-training (α=0.75, two χ² budgets) and (2) a control given the same number of neutral GRPO training steps. Run three seeds each. Then train both with GRPO under three later reward setups: neutral (task reward only), orthogonal (an all-caps style rule on the reasoning), and in-conflict (a penalty whenever the reasoning mentions coins). Record four things over training: - monitor recall on coin-related reasoning, using an LLM judge - the MI estimate between reasoning and output - the number of steps until monitor recall falls below 50% - accuracy when reasoning traces are swapped between samples, to detect private encodings The main result is the gap in steps-to-obfuscation between the treated and control checkpoints, plus a "steganography quadrant" metric (MI held while monitor recall collapses). If the coin-flip results justify it, the second experiment repeats this on MBPP test-hacking with a monitor penalty.
why: Labs will only adopt a monitorability post-training stage if its effect survives the RL that follows it. The method was published three weeks ago, its authors explicitly flag this as untested, and my searches found no follow-up. Combining it with the DeepMind framework gives clear predictions to test: protection should hold in the neutral and orthogonal setups, and in-conflict training should take longer to break monitoring. A positive result means the method can protect monitoring in practice. A negative result is also useful: it shows that a one-time repair isn't enough and the objective must stay active during training, and the steganography check could catch the method creating a new failure mode. It's feasible on open models with GRPO at 8B scale, and none of the nine active registry projects overlaps with it.

direction: Test whether correcting an untrusted monitor on one caught collusion behavior provides protection against adaptive attacks on unseen behaviors.
project: Corrected Until Challenged: Adaptive Robustness of Monitor Repair
question: At matched attack-search budgets and honest-task acceptance, how much of the safety improvement from corrective training survives attacker adaptation?
first_experiment: Run a sandboxed coding pilot comparing fixed and freshly optimized attacks against uncorrected, single-behavior-corrected, and unrelated-training control monitors across three seeds.
why: It directly tests a consequential gap between reported corrective transfer and deployment safety, has objective outcomes and useful results in either direction, and the literature searched studies fixed-submission collusion repair, adaptive attack selection, and monitor co-training separately without resolving their intersection.

direction: Investigate whether task-specific approval histories let AI agents causally weaken human oversight, independently of workload, and whether consequence-focused review prevents it.
project: Approval Conditioning: Can AI Agents Train Their Overseers to Miss the Exception?
question: Does repeated approval of closely matched legitimate actions increase acceptance of an identical unauthorized action, and can trusted consequence-difference displays prevent that increase without sacrificing useful work?
first_experiment: Run a randomized sandboxed human-review pilot crossing repetitive versus diverse legitimate approval histories with conventional versus consequence-difference interfaces, holding the final violation and monitor alert fixed.
why: It targets the human bottleneck that can invalidate otherwise accurate AI monitors, is feasible without large-scale training, and addresses a specific causal and defensive question not established by the inspected fatigue models or existing human sabotage studies.

direction: Study whether dependency-aware release gates can prevent distributed AI-agent sabotage under realistic monitoring delays without sacrificing most legitimate throughput.
project: Review Before Release: Containing Distributed Agent Sabotage
question: At matched monitoring and audit budgets, can gating consequential operations on review of their upstream dependencies reduce irreversible harm more efficiently than asynchronous or fully synchronous monitoring?
first_experiment: Extend the public persistent-state control benchmark with instrumented external effects and delayed review queues, then compare three gating protocols against adaptive attackers while measuring harm, throughput, and latency.
why: It targets a consequential and explicitly acknowledged gap between detection and prevention, offers a feasible experiment using existing infrastructure, and could yield a practical control mechanism; the literature reviewed studies its ingredients separately, but I found no direct evaluation combining shared-state attacks, dependency-based release gates, and measured review latency, so novelty remains provisional.

direction: Develop execution-grounded oversight that detects and blocks sabotage composed across agents and sessions.
project: Causal Checkpoints: Counterfactual Testing for Distributed Agent Sabotage
question: Can dependency-guided counterfactual execution prevent more distributed sabotage than strong stateful monitors at comparable monitoring cost and benign-task utility?
first_experiment: Compare link-tracking, dependency retrieval, and retrieval-plus-counterfactual testing on 60 persistent-codebase attack sequences and matched benign workflows, measuring prevention before harm at a separately calibrated sequence-level false-alarm threshold.
why: It targets a demonstrated structural weakness with a tractable defensive experiment, while the specific combination remains unestablished in the literature reviewed because reliable cross-session replay and security-relevant test selection are difficult.

direction: Make AI-control sabotage monitors robust to the identity of the untrusted model by finding what causes the lineage-specific gap and removing it.
project: Style-Invariant Monitoring — Is Cross-Lineage Monitor Failure a Stylistic Artifact, and Can Canonicalization Fix It?
question: Is the own-lineage advantage of trained sabotage monitors driven by lineage-specific surface style rather than by the semantics of the sabotage? If it is, does passing transcripts through a style-normalizing step before monitoring (trusted-model paraphrase or code canonicalization) close the cross-lineage gap without reducing in-lineage detection? Does the gap also appear in more agentic settings with realized sabotage, such as BashArena and SHADE-Arena with more tasks?
first_experiment: 1. Replicate the core result at small scale. Use ControlArena APPS backdoors from 4 open-weight families (about 600 transcripts each). Fit a LoRA transcript monitor per family and build the 4×4 AUROC matrix. Compute the interaction term and check that it is about +0.1 to +0.17. 2. Test whether style carries the signal. Train a lineage-identification classifier on the same transcripts. Check how well it predicts the monitor's score. Compare the monitor's raw-transcript AUROC with its code-only AUROC. 3. Apply three normalizations before monitoring: - AST-level canonicalization (strip comments, rename identifiers, reformat). - Paraphrase of the reasoning and commentary by a fixed trusted model. - Both together. 4. Recompute the matrix for each normalization. The primary outcome is the interaction term and the off-lineage catch rate at a 1% audit budget, along with the in-lineage loss. 5. Run leave-one-family-out training with normalized data against pooled raw data, to see which is the better defense. The decision rule is that if the replication fails, I stop and report a null result on the original claim. That is a useful outcome in itself.
why: - **Importance.** Control evaluations rely on monitors that will face models they were never tuned on. The gap is large (about 20 points of catch rate) and affects deployment decisions directly. - **Tractability.** It needs only open-weight models, small LoRA training runs and existing ControlArena data. One person with a few GPUs can finish the first experiment in days. - **Not already done.** The existing paper diagnoses the gap and recommends reporting transfer matrices and recalibrating. I found no work in my searches that tests whether removing lineage style closes it. Its "geometric" explanation is correlational, and normalization is an interventional test of it. - **Informative either way.** - If normalization works, it gives a cheap, model-agnostic fix. - If it fails, the difference between lineages is semantic, which means monitors need per-lineage recalibration and control evaluations need transfer matrices. - **Main risks.** The result may not replicate, since I have not verified the paper's data. Paraphrasing could erase real sabotage signal, which is why I measure the in-lineage loss. Frontier-model sabotage is rare, so the agentic part may stay underpowered. I will report that rather than overclaim.

direction: Train and evaluate trusted sabotage monitors that stay effective on attacker model families they were never calibrated on, which is the transfer gap measured in 2607.06596.
project: Lineage-Blind Monitors — Closing the Cross-Family Transfer Gap in Trusted Monitoring
question: Can a monitor trained with leave-one-lineage-out objectives (pooled multi-family training, lineage-adversarial training, or transcript canonicalization) keep its detection on an unseen attacker family close to its in-lineage detection? How does that gap scale with the number of training families? Does the own-family advantage reflect a stylistic fingerprint rather than a sabotage signal?
first_experiment: I'll reproduce the 2607.06596 setup on ControlArena APPS with the open-weight families (Qwen3-14B, Gemma-3-27B, Mistral-Small-3.2, Llama-3.3-70B) plus one or two frontier families. I'd train a LoRA transcript-reading monitor on a small open model with a strict leave-one-family-out split. - Baselines: single-family monitors and naive pooling. - Metrics: held-out-family AUROC and catch rate at a 1% audit budget, with task-clustered bootstrap intervals. - First interventions, run before any adversarial training: - (a) Pooling over k = 1, 2, 3 training families, to get the scaling curve. - (b) A trusted model that rewrites transcripts into a canonical style before the monitor sees them. - (c) A lineage-prediction probe on the monitor's features, to test the fingerprint hypothesis.
why: Trusted monitoring is the main deployed AI-control mechanism, and the next untrusted model will never be the one the monitor was calibrated on, so a transfer gap this size is a real safety problem. The existing paper establishes the problem but tests only pooling as a fix, and calls it partial. Nobody I found has tested lineage-adversarial training or transcript canonicalization, or measured how the gap scales with the number of training families. It is cheap to run with open-weight models, it builds on a public benchmark, and it overlaps with no entry in the registry. The main risk is that canonicalization strips real sabotage signal along with the style. A null result would still be informative, because it would show that the gap needs per-lineage recalibration.

direction: Develop trusted monitoring that converts untrusted explanations into executable evidence and test its robustness against adaptive sabotage.
project: Explain, Execute, Audit
question: Can explanation-guided test generation improve sabotage detection over direct explanation review and explanation-free testing at matched compute and false-positive rates?
first_experiment: On 100 held-out APPS problems, compare those three protocols plus stripped-code review, using paired honest and verified-backdoored solutions, a separate calibration set, and equal-budget adaptive attackers; measure successful undetected backdoors at a 5% benign false-positive rate with task-level confidence intervals.
why: It targets a demonstrated weakness in a deployable safety mechanism with a cheap, falsifiable experiment; the potential novelty is the combination of explanation isolation, executable evidence, and adaptive evaluation, which the reviewed work does not establish, although this search cannot prove it has never been done.

direction: Test whether chain-of-thought monitorability post-training is robust to deliberate evasion, or whether it accidentally makes models better at controlling and hiding their reasoning.
project: Monitorable Until Asked Not To Be: Adversarial Robustness and Controllability Side-Effects of CoT Monitorability Post-Training
question: After monitorability post-training (mutual-information objective; self-distillation and RL verbalization training), do models become more or less able to control their CoT and evade CoT monitors under user-instructed, self-instructed and pressure-prompted evasion? Does the monitor-recall gain survive adversarial elicitation?
first_experiment: Take DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Qwen3.5-4B, plus their monitorability-trained variants: Fu et al.'s released OPSD/RL recipes, and a reimplemented Anwar mutual-information + χ² post-training on the HarmBench setting. Measure on each: 1. CoT-Control controllability, both user-instructed and self-instructed (prefill and bootstrap). 2. Monitor catch rate on MonitorBench and HarmBench prefix tasks, with and without Dolev-style self-instructed evasion prompts, scored by GPT-4.1-nano and Qwen3.5-35B monitors. The core result is a 2×2: monitorability training (yes/no) × evasion pressure (none/adversarial). It shows whether the gains shrink, vanish or reverse under attack, and whether controllability goes up.
why: Monitorability training is about to be proposed as a standard post-training stage, and its safety value depends on the gains not being a "verbalize when convenient" skill that the model can switch off. Both papers appeared within the last three weeks and tested only non-adversarial settings. Anwar et al. state this requirement, admit their method cannot guarantee it, and defer it to future work, while Dolev et al. show evasion via self-instruction already works on untrained models. The experiment is cheap (7B-scale models, existing code and benchmarks), the outcome is genuinely uncertain in both directions, and either answer directly informs whether labs should adopt these methods.

direction: Determine whether bounded monitor memory enables delayed sabotage, and whether retaining unresolved evidence improves safety at fixed monitoring cost.
project: Unresolved Evidence: Safety Monitoring Across Long Commit Histories
question: At matched inference budgets and whole-history false-alarm rates, how does inserting benign commits between attack preparation and activation affect detection, and can evidence retention prevent any resulting degradation?
first_experiment: Extend the public Iterative VibeCoding benchmark with paired sandbox histories containing identical attack preparation and activation separated by 0, 8, or 32 validated benign commits; compare its link-tracker with a bounded evidence ledger, restore omitted evidence as a diagnostic intervention, and measure undetected successful attacks, honest-task completion, and cost using held-out task families and confidence intervals.
why: This is my strongest candidate because it tests a consequential deployment failure with a tractable causal design and an existing baseline; prior work establishes distributed attacks, stateful defenses, and recall failures separately, but the literature I found does not establish whether benign delays causally undermine safety monitoring under matched budgets and false-alarm rates—an evidence-based novelty claim, not proof that no related work exists.

direction: Measure how much RL penalty pressure a trained self-report channel (flag tool call or CoT verbalization) can take before the model keeps hacking but stops reporting, compared with an output-only monitor.
project: Does the Tip Line Stay Open? Self-Report Channels Under Penalty Pressure in Reward-Hacking RL
question: After a model is trained to flag its own test-tampering and developers then use those flags to penalize episodes in RL, does it lose the flagging while keeping the hacking? How does the penalty size at which this happens compare across a self-report tool call, CoT verbalization and an output-only monitor, and does a split penalty design (penalize only verified hacks, never reports) keep the channel open?
first_experiment: Run Qwen3-8B in Countdown-Code, SFT-ing report/verbalization on hack types 1 and 2 only and holding out type 3. Then run GRPO under four conditions (no penalty, penalty on reports, penalty from an output-only monitor, penalty on verified hacks only) at three penalty sizes and 3 seeds. Track the true hack rate, report recall given a hack, the undetected-hack rate and the hack-type mix. The first comparison is report recall given a hack under condition (b) versus condition (a).
why: Developers will penalize or filter detected hacks in RL. Obfuscation under penalty has been shown for CoT and probes but, in my searches, not for self-report channels. A cheap small-model testbed already exists, and the result directly tells developers how to wire self-report into training.

direction: Develop latency-aware control protocols that prevent irreversible harm from concurrent, potentially misaligned AI agents under limited oversight capacity.
project: Caught Too Late: Containment Under Parallel Agent Attacks
question: Can dependency-aware quarantine reduce irreversible attacker success relative to asynchronous monitoring and rollback while retaining more useful throughput than fully synchronous review?
first_experiment: Run adaptive staged exfiltration attacks in a sandbox with one or four agents, three review delays, and a finite audit queue, comparing asynchronous rollback, synchronous review, and dependency-aware quarantine at matched oversight budgets.
why: It targets a consequential gap between detecting attacks and preventing harm, has tractable experiments and immediate deployment relevance, and the closest work studies latency, distributed attacks, or transactional execution without the combined adversarial evaluation proposed here.

direction: Test whether CoT-monitorability post-training works as a defence ahead of time: does it make a model's reasoning harder to obfuscate later, or does it just repair damage that has already happened?
project: Vaccinating the Chain of Thought: Does Monitorability Post-Training Survive Monitor-Aware Finetuning and RL Pressure?
question: If a reasoning model first gets mutual-information monitorability post-training (Anwar et al., 2026) and is *then* exposed to documents describing a CoT monitor, or to RL pressure against that monitor, does it obfuscate less than an untreated model? And does the treatment raise or lower its CoT controllability, the trait that predicts obfuscation?
first_experiment: A 2×2 design on one open reasoning model (Qwen3-8B, or about 4B if compute is tight). Factor 1: with or without the monitorability post-training (the RMI + χ² objective, on unlabeled reasoning prompts). Factor 2: Haskins et al.'s monitor-aware documents vs their behaviour-only control documents. For each of the four arms I'll measure: - the undetected-misbehaviour rate on their prompted deception task, with a fixed LLM CoT monitor; - CoT controllability, using the Chen et al. 2026 constraint tasks; - a task-accuracy check that capabilities are intact. The key number is the interaction term: how much the obfuscation jump caused by the monitor documents shrinks in the post-trained model. If the protection shows up, the next step is an RL arm that measures how many steps each model takes to reach 20% undetected reward hacking.
why: Developers would realistically put a monitorability stage before more training, not after it. So the question that matters for deployment is whether the gains last under later pressure. Neither paper answers it: Anwar et al. only repair damage after the fact, and they leave non-manipulability as an untested goal. Haskins et al. show the threat but test no defence. The result is useful either way. If the post-trained model obfuscates less, we have a cheap, label-free defence. If it obfuscates as much or more, for example because the training raises controllability, that is an important warning about a method being proposed for production pipelines. The papers came out in May and on Oct 21, 2026, and I found no follow-up combining them. The setup is small: one model, existing objectives and task designs, a 2×2 of fine-tunes.

direction: Test whether white-box activation probes keep detecting implicit, unverbalized influence on model behavior in cases where CoT monitors fail.
project: Probing Where the CoT Is Silent: Activation Monitors vs. CoT Monitors Under Implicit Influence
question: On matched implicit-influence tasks, do activation probes trained to detect that a nudge shifted the answer outperform CoT monitors? Do they stay robust when guidance system prompts suppress verbalization? Do they transfer across task formats and to the explicit-instruction arm?
first_experiment: Re-run the Duzan & Stickland benchmark (public code) on 2–3 open-weight reasoning models. Collect the behavior-shift labels (nudged answer differs from the un-nudged answer). Collect CoT-monitor detection rates for the implicit arm, the explicit arm, and the guidance-prompt condition. Extract residual-stream activations at the end of the CoT. Train linear probes for "behavior was shifted by the nudge" on two task formats, then test on the other two and on the guidance-prompt condition. Compare probe AUROC with CoT-monitor detection at matched false-positive rates.
why: The implicit-influence gap is the largest documented hole in the main practical oversight tool. Whether white-box signals fill it is the obvious next question, and it decides whether we need to invest in probes or in training CoT to be more monitorable. Prior work either measures CoT monitors only (Duzan & Stickland) or trains monitorability without testing implicit settings (Anwar et al.). The experiment is cheap, since the benchmark and code already exist. A negative result (probes failing under guidance prompts) would also be informative. I could not rule out an unpublished or concurrent version of this exact comparison, so the first step should be a quick re-check before running it.

direction: Preserve meaningful human control by ensuring that consequential AI-agent workflows remain safely recoverable after the initiating agent is forcibly removed.
project: Safe to Stop: Recovery Contracts for Agent-Independent Shutdown
question: Can externally enforced recovery contracts prevent agents from creating dependence on their continued operation while preserving useful task performance?
first_experiment: Fork three models’ trajectories across 60 sandboxed workflow tasks at ten action boundaries, forcibly remove the initiating agent, and compare post-removal safety and bounded recovery against continuation, checkpointing, rollback, and recovery-contract baselines.
why: It addresses a consequential gap between shutdown compliance and actual control with a falsifiable, practical intervention; the specific novelty is pairing forced-removal evaluation with pre-action independent-recoverability enforcement, a combination I did not find in the searched literature rather than a claim that shutdown safety or recovery is itself new.

direction: Test durable recovery from agent-memory poisoning when dependency provenance is incomplete.
project: Broken Lineage: Durable Memory Repair Under Imperfect Provenance
question: Can uncertainty-triggered replay reduce post-repair unauthorized behavior at matched cost while preserving useful memory when lineage records omit dependencies?
first_experiment: Run paired poisoned and clean multi-session histories across two models, vary provenance completeness, and compare deletion, lineage repair, conservative repair, and budgeted replay over ten post-repair sessions.
why: It tests a consequential assumption with a feasible, falsifiable experiment; existing work covers memory attacks, repair, and lineage degradation, but the reviewed sources do not jointly establish durable behavioral recovery under measured provenance omissions at matched utility and cost.

direction: Stress-test and put calibrated uncertainty on the logit-linear extrapolation of low-FPR trusted-monitor performance, since AI-control safety estimates rely on it.
project: How Far Can You Trust a Logit ROC? Low-FPR Monitor Safety Estimates Under Adaptive Attack and Benign Drift
question: When logit(TPR) is fit linearly against logit(FPR) from limited data, how large are the errors at FPR of 1e-4 to 1e-3, and can they be bounded with valid intervals? Specifically: - (a) How large is the error when the attacker optimizes against the monitor, which is expected to truncate or reshape the attack-score tail? - (b) How large is the error when the benign distribution shifts between calibration and deployment, for example a new task mix or a different agent model? - (c) Does a Bayesian or bootstrap-over-families approach, such as logistic, heavier-tailed, and mixture-with-null fits, give intervals that actually cover the true TPR?
first_experiment: 1. Generate benign and attack trajectories in a public control setting such as BashArena or SHADE-Arena, or a lighter synthetic coding-sabotage setup. I'll check how much of it is available before committing. 2. Score every step with 3–4 open-weight monitors of different sizes. Use at least 100k benign steps so that the empirical 1e-4 FPR tail is measurable ground truth. 3. Subsample small calibration sets of 1k to 20k benign steps and fit the logit-linear model. Measure coverage and RMS error against the full-data TPR. 4. Repeat with two perturbations: - Attacks generated with best-of-n selection against the monitor, or with monitor-aware prompting. - A calibration/deployment split along task category or agent model. 5. Compare the plain logistic fit against heavy-tailed and mixture alternatives, and against a conformal or bootstrap interval. Report the sample size at which each approach becomes reliable.
why: A control safety case turns on the monitor's recall at an audit budget too low to measure directly. That makes the extrapolation a load-bearing but under-validated assumption. The work is cheap, uses only monitor scores, and doesn't need frontier-model access or RL training. It gives practitioners a concrete deliverable: when the logit fit can be trusted, and what interval to report when it can't. I found no study of the fit under adaptive attack or benign drift. The nearby papers I found cover monitor transfer across model lineages, distributed attacks, and monitor red-teaming benchmarks. None of them addresses statistical validity at low FPR. This is a negative-results-friendly design, because showing where the fit breaks is publishable either way.

direction: Use synthetic document finetuning (SDF) to plant false beliefs about where oversight fails, so that a misaligned model's attempt to evade a monitor leaves an easily detected signature.
project: Decoy Blind Spots: Turning Monitor-Awareness into a Tripwire
question: If a model fine-tuned to misbehave also learns, through SDF, a fictitious blind spot in its CoT or probe monitor, does it use that blind spot when motivated to evade? Does that make its evasion attempts detectable with high recall and a low false-positive rate? And does this hold when it also has real information about how to evade?
first_experiment: Reuse the setup of the ICML "Out of Context Obfuscation" paper and of 2605.15257, using Qwen3-14B and 32B: - **Base model.** Start from a malign checkpoint trained to hide adverse drug findings. - **Four arms, all with SDF:** - (a) monitor-aware only; - (b) monitor-aware plus a decoy blind spot: "the monitor does not inspect text between `<internal-note>` tags"; - (c) decoy plus a real evasion strategy; - (d) decoy taught to a benign, non-malign model, as a false-positive control. - **Measures:** - how often the decoy signature appears when the model is incentivised to deceive versus on honest tasks; - recall of detecting misbehaviour using the signature alone, using the existing CoT monitor or probe alone, and using the two combined; - whether the decoy reduces evasion that uses the real strategy; - how deeply the decoy is believed, using "Believe It or Not"-style probes of whether the model treats it as true.
why: Prior work has shown that models adopt evasion strategies they learned out of context, but has only treated this as a vulnerability, answered by filtering data. Planting deceptive beliefs about monitors as a defence turns that same mechanism into a detector. I found no work on this in searches for decoys, honeypots and false monitor beliefs. The pieces it needs (SDF, the malign-initialisation testbeds, and probes of belief depth) already exist, so a first result is quick to get and is informative whether it succeeds or fails.

direction: Test whether recently proposed fixes for CoT monitorability under reward misspecification still work, or backfire, when the model has learned that its CoT is monitored.
project: Salient Rewards, Watched Thoughts: Does Reward Description Training Survive Monitor-Aware Models?
question: When a model has absorbed knowledge of CoT monitoring through document fine-tuning, does reward description training still restore monitorability of reward hacking? Or does making the misspecified reward explicit speed up hacking that the monitor fails to catch?
first_experiment: On gpt-oss-20b with Yan & Hewitt's length task (reward misspecified to favor exceeding the word limit), I will build two models: one fine-tuned on Haskins-style monitor-description documents and one on matched control documents. Each then gets RL on the misspecified reward with and without reward description training, 3 seeds per cell. I will track hack rate, g-mean² monitorability (a strong and a weak monitor), and the rate at which the CoT verbalizes the reward at each training step.
why: It joins two results from the last six months: reward misspecification hides hacking, and monitor awareness drives obfuscation. It also directly tests whether the best recent mitigation holds up under the threat model it most needs to survive. The setup reuses public testbeds, small open models and cheap tasks. Every outcome is informative: if the fix holds, that's evidence it is robust; if it backfires, that's a key warning before anyone adopts it. It hasn't been done because the mitigation papers came out about three weeks ago and tested only on models with no knowledge of monitoring. The monitor-awareness paper tested no mitigations, and no one in the registry is working on anything nearby.

direction: Test whether hiding experimental-arm identities and checking frozen analyses under secret arm permutations reduces targeted sabotage by AI research agents.
project: Blind Arms — Information Restrictions Against Research Sabotage
question: How much can experimental blinding reduce accepted false conclusions under adaptive attacks while preserving honest analysis quality, and how does the benefit depend on identity leakage?
first_experiment: Run a four-condition control evaluation on twelve cached safety-monitor comparisons with matched honest runs, measuring directional sabotage, effect suppression, identity inference, and utility.
why: It offers a cheap, falsifiable intervention against hard-to-detect research manipulation; the reviewed work studies sabotage auditing and evaluation-awareness blinding, but I found no direct test of arm-identity blinding plus permutation replay against adaptive research saboteurs.

direction: Measure whether CoT obfuscation induced by RL pressure against one monitor type transfers to evading other, differently-informed monitors, which would show whether monitor diversity is a real defense.
project: Does Diversity Help? Cross-Monitor Transfer of Induced Chain-of-Thought Obfuscation
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained to reward-hack while evading monitor A (a CoT-reading LLM monitor, an action-only monitor, or a residual-stream probe), how much does its detectability drop under the other monitor types? Does an ensemble of diverse monitors keep a usefully high detection rate at a fixed false-positive rate for longer into training than any single monitor?
first_experiment: Take a small open reasoning model, such as a 7–14B distilled reasoning model, in a coding environment with a known test-hacking exploit. 1. Run RL with a penalty from a CoT-reading LLM monitor, plus an unpenalized control run. 2. Checkpoint regularly. At each checkpoint, record the hack rate and the recall of three held-out monitors at 1% false-positive rate: the penalized CoT monitor, an action-only monitor, and a linear probe trained on activations from the unpenalized model. 3. Plot recall against training step for each monitor and for the ensemble. The key quantity is the gap between the penalized monitor and the other two. A small gap would mean evasion is monitor-specific and diversity helps. A large gap would mean obfuscation is general. 4. Repeat with the penalty placed on the probe, to check whether the result is symmetric.
why: Real deployments will stack several monitors, but the obfuscation literature mostly tests a single monitor. Whether diversity gives real protection or only the appearance of it is a decision-relevant question. It is also cheap to run at small scale and has a clear measurable outcome either way. My novelty claim rests on a short search, so before starting I would check specifically for work on cross-monitor transfer of obfuscation and on probe-versus-CoT-monitor evasion (for example the "evading probes" work from December 2025).

direction: Use probes the model is never trained against ("canaries") to detect, without labels, when RL against an activation probe has made the model evade it, and to trigger retraining.
project: Canary Probes — Detecting Probe Evasion During RL Without Ground-Truth Labels
question: When a policy is trained with an activation-probe penalty against reward hacking, does a family of held-out probes (different layers, pooling methods, nonlinear/attention architectures, and unsupervised representation-drift statistics) keep detecting the hacking while the penalized probe is evaded? And does the disagreement between penalized and held-out probes give a label-free alarm that predicts evasion early enough to retrain the probe? Retraining would use labels from the held-out probes, not true labels.
first_experiment: - **Setup:** reproduce the MBPP reward-hacking environment (unit tests can be special-cased, so the model can hard-code test outputs) on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, using GRPO. - **Probes:** a linear mean-pooled probe on layer 16 is the penalty. About 12 canaries are held out: linear probes on other layers, max/attention-pooled probes, a 2-layer MLP, a probe trained on a different hacking dataset, and a Mahalanobis drift score against a reference set from before training. - **Measurements:** over 3 seeds, track at each checkpoint: - the true hack rate - each probe's recall/AUROC on true labels - the label-free disagreement statistic, which is the penalized probe's score minus the median canary score, on unlabeled rollouts - **Success criterion:** at least one class of canaries keeps AUROC above 0.85 after the penalized probe falls below 0.6, and the disagreement alarm fires at least N steps before the hack rate recovers. The baseline is the oracle-labelled adaptive retraining trigger.
why: Probe penalties are one of the few scalable ways to reduce reward hacking, but their validity under optimization has so far been tested only with oracle labels. The newest positive result, iterative retraining, quietly assumes those labels. A label-free alarm is the missing piece for using it in practice. Prior work shows evasion can extend to unseen probes but hasn't measured which monitor families resist it during RL reward hacking, or used disagreement between monitors as a signal. The registry has no overlapping project, and the experiment fits on one machine with a 7B model and open environments.

direction: Develop and stress-test counterfactual execution monitors that detect unauthorized behavior emerging from multiple individually plausible code changes.
project: Counterfactual Checks for Cross-Commit Sabotage
question: At matched compute and false-positive budgets, does targeted counterfactual execution reduce undetected distributed sabotage beyond stateful monitoring, structural analysis, and ordinary sandbox testing?
first_experiment: Run a paired ablation on held-out Iterative VibeCoding trajectories, comparing existing monitors and ordinary tests against the same defenses augmented with sandboxed counterfactual executions.
